subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, June 14, consideration of the motion of Miss MacDonald (for the Minister of State (Finance)) that Bill C-51, an Act to provide borrowing authority, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to resume debate from last Friday. At that time I was indicating that the Government's Budget resembled A Tale of Two Cities. One city is the shining city on the Hill in which the Government sees the economy improving and an economic state which is progressing well. The other city reflects the other side of the tracks that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) and the Government have difficulty understanding.
If the Government understood these problems, it would not have imposed the partial deindexation of old age pensions for seniors across the country. It would not ask consumers to pay 2 cents a litre more to make up for the shortfall as a result of what was given to the multinational oil companies. It would not have cut nearly $100 million in job training programs. It would not have increased sales tax across the board, which is a very regressive step. It would not have asked families with two children who earn between $15,000 and $20,000 annually to pay 36 per cent more tax by the year 1990 while the $200,000 family with two children is looking simply at a 2 per cent raise in their taxes.
The Government would show that it is beginning to understand this other city if it were to forget its obsession with the deficit and introduce job creation programs in order to put Canadians back to work. However, the Budget is simply bankrupt of any new or worth-while job creation initiatives.
Without a job, an individual loses that sense of dignity and purpose. As a result, the country loses that same sense of dignity and purpose. That is the tale of the city which the Government has failed to recognize.
Certainly nothing depicts that better than the Government's attack on senior citizens by partially removing the full indexation that they thought was theirs. One of the measurements of
a progressive, mature and compassionate country is to see how its society treats its senior citizens. Certainly, with the Budget proposal to deindex partially senior citizens old age pensions, we cannot say that we are as progressive and compassionate as we would like to believe.
However, the Government can vindicate itself and correct the wrong. In order to do so, the Prime Minister and the Government must understand the other city to which I have referred. It is one in which there are more poor than ever, more families in financial trouble and where the line-ups at the food bank and soup kitchens are increasing. It is a city in which there is an increasing need for shelters for the homeless and where thousands of young people have less opportunity to find their first jobs. It is a city where students cannot afford the tuition for their education and the unemployed cannot change their fate despite their efforts.
Ottawa may well be the shining city on the Hill and one may get a good view from 24 Sussex, but one cannot see from there the other city in which thousands of Canadians live. The Prime Minister must visit this other city to see the despair painted on people's faces. The concern of the unemployed worker in Sault Ste. Marie must become his concern. The problems facing the high school graduate who cannot afford to enroll at York University must become his problem. The struggle of an elderly disabled person in Sarnia must become his struggle. The future of a woman in Hamilton striving to find her rightful place in the work world must become his future. Our failure to have compassion and understanding for these dilemmas facing Canadians will be our misgiving and a failure of our country to react to a situation that needs attention.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to Bill C-51 with decidedly mixed feelings. No one would question the need for borrowing authority in present circumstances. However, the extent of the borrowing authority can be criticized, and in that respect I want to explore that situation in the time available to me this morning.
The Bill seeks to authorize the borrowing of $18.2 billion, only $16 billion of which is money that is directly required for this year. The other $2.2 billion is designed to cover borrowing that was made necessary last winter because of the actions of the Liberal majority in the Senate.
My colleagues and I are justly critical of the need for that borrowing to cover action under Section 39 of the Financial Administration Act. If we had no Senate there would not have

June 17, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
been a need for that part of the borrowing authority that we are debating and eventually voting on.
However, I believe there are deeper reasons for being critical of the Bill before us. It is, in a sense, dealing with the bottom line in the country's accounts, in the Government's financial operations. It is here that decisions on taxation and expenditure come out. It is here that one has to provide the funds required to make up the shortfall in taxation which will be required if the Government is to carry on operations for the coming year.
I want to consider both the possibility that sounder fiscal policies on the taxation side would have made necessary a smaller borrowing and, without meaning to contradict that conclusion, to consider the possibility that the kinds of development policies Canada needs in the present depressed circumstances might well call for larger borrowings than the Government is in fact undertaking. Before beginning that explanation, I might note that the borrowing authority Bill has been brought in properly, as we had arranged in December that it should be, at a time when the Government was considering a very large Bill covering this year in quite an inappropriate way. Our opposition persuaded the Government to break down the matter into other Bills. Within days after the Budget had been brought down in the House on May 23, on May 28, the Bill came before us for first reading. That appropriate action is one I want to recognize.
In considering the weaknesses of the Budget on the taxation side, I should like to indicate the first aspect of weakness which concerns me in this borrowing authority consideration and to compare this Budget with Budgets of recent years and with Budgets of the early 1930s when another Conservative Government had to deal with the problems of Depression and did so in many ways by actions which are quite similar to the ones this Government has undertaken in 1984-85. Of course, at that time revenues fell off sharply. The Customs Tariff was a much larger part of the basis of income for Government. Obviously that would fall off as trade values decreased and trade declined. Revenues fell off in sales tax and excise taxes, with only income tax seeming to be a sound basis for the Government to predict what its revenues would actually be.
In those days, Finance Ministers were as determined to balance the Budget as is the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). Of course it was not possible to take in enough in taxation to cover the relief costs and certain public works expenditures, which somewhat compensated for declining private sector activity. However, certainly every attempt was made to try to cover the costs of the ordinary operations of Government.
I have just referred to some public works expenditures. At the beginning of that Government's administration there was a good deal of public works authorization, but that fell off very rapidly. By 1932 and 1933, the Bennett Government was behaving very much the way the present Government is behaving. It was involved in a decrease of public works activities and
in an increase in various taxes. Interestingly enough, sales tax was put on ice-cream cones and other things back in 1932, in the same way the present Minister of Finance has decided to tax various confectionary and drugstore products. The refusal to make any significant change in the tax system in those days was very much like the determination of the present Minister of Finance to leave the basic structure of taxation unchanged. There was, interestingly enough, in the very first Budget brought down by R. B. Bennett as both Minister of Finance and Prime Minister, a rejoicing in foreign investment, specifically the American investment which had come into Canada in the first months after his Government took office. In fact, the Budget Speech contains a long list of enterprises, practically all of them in Ontario and Quebec, which presumably represented some triumph of Conservative policy as early as 193031. All of this was carried out in the context of what a Minister of Finance, looking back in 1933, characterized as being done against the backdrop of the dead hand of past lavish expenditures and borrowing, by Liberal Governments, of course. If that kind of phrase does not evoke the spirit of the present Government's fiscal policy and attitude, I cannot imagine what would.
M5)
Perhaps the most striking contrast between the Budgets of those days and the Budget which we heard on May 23 of this year is the fact that the Government recognized that the wealthy should bear their fair share of the burden of government. Consequently, year by year, the income tax increased. It may astound my colleagues across the way to realize that by 1933 millionaires in Canada were paying income tax of more than 50 per cent. The actual tax bill for someone with $1 million of income in 1933-34 exceeded $500,000. That is the kind of taxation which allows a Government to try to cover the costs of its normal activities. It was of course not sufficient to cover the development needs the country had.
The Budget also talked about the irresponsible borrowing patterns of the past 10 years and excoriated the excesses of Liberal Governments in the past for their lavish expenditure and the consequent borrowing needs. The sad reality of this Budget, of course, is that the patterns it follows are so largely the budget patterns of years past, that is, the Liberal policy of trying to shift the burden of taxation to individuals and allowing all sorts of tax breaks to corporations. Those patterns are certainly followed in this Budget, excessively so on the individual's side. The hope that it will increase economic activity and lead to jobs is one which past Governments have expressed in a series of Budgets. The Budgets of Marc Lalonde and Allan MacEachen certainly expressed those hopes. The consequent failure of those hopes, the failure to move any closer to full employment, the run-up of large deficits and the resulting need to borrow are quite in keeping with what the present Government holds out to us. What we have then, surely, in this Budget is no departure from the past.
Conservative Members have moved to government benches and taken up Liberal ideas, which they of course evinced often enough when they were voting on Budgets in the past in
June 17, 1985

support of a Liberal Government. One wonders, then, how we can break out of the situation we are in if then Liberal and now Conservative policies do not do it. I want to suggest that, on the one hand, there be a thorough reconsideration and reform of our taxation system. This would provide us with a basis for raising far more revenue and allow us to readjust the burden of taxation in such a way that we would give a strong and healthy stimulus to the economy which, accompanied by other policies, could ensure that Canadian citizens would be able to give that impetus to the private sector, the small and large businesses which the Government talks about so much. There, it seems to me, is the Budget's most overwhelming failure. I recognize deindexation as being a political blunder of the largest scale. The Government now realizes that as well.
The failure to deal with tax reform and in fact the rejection of any kind of massive tax reform by the Minister of Finance is far-reaching and touches the lives of all Canadians. The Budget in its fiscal projections recognizes that the revenues of the Government will come in the proportion of 45 cents from individual taxpayers and only 15 cents from corporations. The balance that prevailed within the last quarter century when corporations paid rather more to Ottawa than individuals has now shifted so far that individuals pay three times as much in taxation to Ottawa as corporations. When we recognize that there has been that kind of shift in the taxation system of the country, we can recognize the hand of excessive and outrageous taxation of individuals which leaves individuals unable to support fundamentally their households and therefore unable to produce the impetus that is required for a sound economy to develop in this country again.
The failure of the Conservative Government to make any progress in the taxation system by loading even more taxation on poor and middle-income Canadians while leaving the rich even less burdened with taxation creates the kind of imbalance in which the fiscal statements of the country become a means for enriching some and impoverishing others. It seems to me that that makes this a Government which speaks for the wealthy in a way that the voters across Canada did not foresee when they voted for Conservatives on September 4. It seems to me that that is a ticking time bomb that deserves to go off in Government ranks sooner rather than later.
That is the fiscal side of the borrowing coin. If the Government allows those billions of dollars of tax breaks and refuses to collect taxes, it will inevitably have to borrow. If Canadians were to realize the amount of money that has gone into businesses through tax breaks, the extent to which ordinary Canadians pay interest on the investment capital of companies rather than having them depend on the stock exchanges and brokerage houses on Bay Street, St. James Street and beyond, and that Liberals and Conservatives have burdened them with paying for the capital for business investment, we would see a revolt of the proportions at which senior citizens have only begun to hint. That, then, is one of the reasons for borrowing. It is sad to say that there has been no fundamental shift in the attitude of Conservative Members.
Borrowing Authority Act
On the other side of the borrowing coin, there has been no real consideration of the development needs of this country. I feel for the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), recognizing what he once did as a Member of the last successful Conservative Government of 1957 to 1963. At that time, national development programs of all sorts were developed. It was a Government of which Canadians could be proud because of its vision of what this country should be. For all of its failures, and some of those failures were failure to act on those national development programs, that Government had a vision for this country. These days, in the most despicable and contemptible way, we have a Government that hopes it can ride on the coat-tails of the American recovery which has been flagging these days, and that suggests that we will continue with the recession. We have a Government which thinks that foreign investors will save Canada. No Canadian can be proud of that. The Minister of "Regional Industrial Stagnation" takes pride in the Government's reduction of support for the shipbuilding industry. The day after the Budget was brought down, the shipbuilding industry was told that the subsidy program would be discontinued. That program has been important to the industry. The Government also cancelled the productivity improvement grant, which was about the only thing that was left for the shipbuilding industry, other than the tariff. A Minister of that sort does not deserve to be in a Canadian Government at a time of depression.
Canada has other needs. I would like to deal with the need for housing. We are falling further and further behind in the housing industry. Canada requires tens of thousands of housing units. I would suggest that the Government look at cooperative housing. That type of housing is the most efficient and socially sensible way of providing housing. It is a context in which people can establish the community and become involved in the committee and board structure. Canadians could begin to pull themselves together sufficiently enough to enter the job market. Co-operative housing suffered at the hands of the Liberal Government. So far it is not doing much better. However, I do not want to speak very severely to this issue because the Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight) who is responsible for housing has a sensitivity for it. Will he be provided with the funds? Will the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation have the means to undertake the housing programs which Canada needs? It is not clear that it will have the funds. Fiscal measures such as the capital gains tax holiday are likely to increase the cost of land and housing. Therefore, CMHC policies which gear income to the market will be more difficult.
The Budget is designed to make things more difficult for the people of Thunder Bay. The waiting lists for housing are very long in Thunder Bay. The people of that community are seeking better and reasonably priced housing. We are not experiencing the general impetus that residential housing construction could provide from coast to coast. That would put people back to work, and it would produce a sound demand for small and large businesses.

June 17, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
The Government has failed to recognize the developing needs of Canada and to respond in an imaginative manner. The Minister of "Regional Industrial Stagnation" takes pride in packaging a variety of principles from years past in a document which requires agreement among all Governments. There may be something to be said for agreement on a statement of principles, not that there is anything remarkable about the details. Beyond that, will we have policy development which is applicable to industries and communities? Will there be financial assistance? Giving tax breaks is the easiest way to go. The distressing thing about tax breaks is that one does not have the means by which to assess their effectiveness and to recognize the cost.
We will vote against the borrowing authority Bill for a variety of reasons. The Government needs borrowing authority because it has failed to tax properly. The Government needs the money because it has failed to develop the kind of policies which Canada needs to get businesses moving and to get people back to work. The failures of the Government in its Budget are just as clear in the borrowing authority Bill as they are in various other areas.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Eton. Member referred to trade with the United States. Does the Hon. Member have any opinions regarding the recent protectionist tariff policy of the U.S. Government as it relates to Canadian products? I refer, Mr. Speaker, specifically to protectionist measures on hogs, lumber, footwear, raspberries and saltfish which, of course, affect the riding of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) just as much as they affect Newfoundland and all the Maritime Provinces. It is an absolutely outrageous protectionist tariff of 20 per cent on the export of these products into the United States from Newfoundland and from the north shore of Quebec. This tariff was imposed last Thursday evening. I am wondering whether the Hon. Member would have any thoughts on the subject as it relates to the policy of free trade which this Government announced. And is this really free trade when it is free for the Americans only but Canadians have to pay 20 cents on the dollar? Why is all of this happening now with the advent of this new Conservative Government?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is a very good question. The desire of Canadians to have free trade with the United States is older than the Dominion of Canada.
1 think of a Conservative Minister of a little more than a hundred years ago who spoke in terms of reciprocity of trade or reciprocity of tariffs. The desire of Canadians and their Government to achieve freer trade agreements with the United States has usually been a desire which Americans have failed to entertain. I suppose the year 1911 would be the main exception when an American Congress and an American administration was suddenly ready for the negotiation of a freer trade agreement with Canada, a significant agreement,
and the Canadian people turned it down at, we might remind ourselves, the behest of the Conservative Party of the day through an unholy alliance with nationalist interests in Quebec which were also fighting the Liberal Government's naval policy at the time. The desire to achieve freer trade arrangements with the United States, then, is an almost universal Canadian desire. In this century, of course, we have become concerned about maintaining economic activity in this country which has been built up at much cost and great pain because the Americans would not allow us to trade freely with themselves.
I think what the American Congress is doing these days in one area or another, Mr. Speaker, is demonstrating again the protectionist tendencies which have been so strong in that body time after time and term after term. We, for our part, can succeed only in minimizing the damage in one area or another. We have worked hard in the area of lumber exports to keep that particular trade open. That is one item in the Hon. Member's list which, I suppose, is directly relevant to northwestern Ontario. But it takes inordinate effort to achieve some opening in the American market for these products.
I am sorry to say that, aside from much determination and all the lobbying efforts we can make in Washington with Members of Congress, there is nothing more 1 can offer the Hon. Member whose constituents are now affected by a tariff on saltfish. We will have to work as hard as we can and remind the Americans of those freer trade traditions which they came to after the Second World War on which, I hope, enough of them still believe their prosperity after the Second World War was based. And we must maintain our pressure on them for freer trade.
Long ago we Canadians settled on reciprocity of tariffs because we could not get reciprocity of trade with the Americans. We should remind the Americans that we do not want to be driven to reciprocity of tariffs at a time when we have in fact been reducing our tariffs and opening our economy more and more to the rest of the world. We should press the United States not only to stop these attempts to put quotas, tariffs and other restrictions on Canadian natural products, a battle which takes us back at least to the 1840s or 1850s, but we should in fact press them in other ways to open the state economies and various industries to Canadian production. We must convince the United States to lessen those "Buy America" policies. We would like to be sure that as much as possible industries which produce, for example, rail rolling stock, city streetcars and subway systems, such as, for example, the CanCar rail plant in Thunder Bay, can produce these systems in our country and that we are not forced by other rules of the United States to manufacture them in the United States, therefore getting some of the earnings back to this country but not the employment which we need so desperately.
I am sorry I do not have any additional solutions at the moment for the Hon. Member except to say that we must press on and remind our friends in Government that the rhetoric we are hearing now will not in fact bring us anything
June 17, 1985

without a great deal of hard work, and even the hard work may not do the job.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister of Canada met with the President of the United States at Quebec City. The Prime Minister at that time informed his constituents- because they were affected-of the pending tariffs which were to be imposed, the tariffs which were under consideration by, I think, the United States International Trade Commission at that time. Yet, in spite of the discussion of the Prime Minister with the President of the United States, which was verified by the Prime Minister publicly in responding to his constituents- and, of course, that matter affected my constituents and a lot of constituencies right throughout eastern Canada-and in spite of the intervention by the Prime Minister, last Thursday night the United States Government imposed that atrocious tariff. It appears that all the representations, which were supposedly to have been made by the Minister of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) together with the Prime Minister, have had no effect whatsoever on the imposition of these tariffs.
So I would like to ask the Hon. Member, in light of what he was saying, whether or not he believes that intervention at the policitical level has any effect at all on general U.S. trade policy as it relates to protectionist tariffs? Historically speaking, would he say, for example, that once that trend is in place, not even the politicians can stop it?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my good friend for another splendid question. What one can derive in the way of lessons from the experience of the late 1940s would suggest one particular word of wisdom for the Government in its present circumstances. I am saying that against the background which my friend has evoked of the summit of the Prime Minister with the President of the United States in which it was suggested that all sorts of good things will follow from the fine relations between the two countries. What Canadians so often forget-and I trust the Prime Minister knows better-is that the American constitution provides for a division of power in which the President has limited authority on many of these matters. He certainly faces the actions of a Congress made up of hundreds of Members representing their districts from coast to coast, and two Senators from every state, all of whom will go their own way. The President might conceivably have the best of intentions, but if those Congressmen do not agree with the decisions he has arrived at, he will not get anywhere.
I think of the late 1940s. The key point in the circumstances of 1947 through 1949 was that the dealings from executive to executive were not nearly as effective by themselves as the Government's holding out the prospect, or the fear, to the American administration and to Congress that the Canadian response in the way of trade restraints, which would be made necessary by our shortage of American dollars at the time, would have a very serious effect in one area or another of the United States. In each of those areas where a congressional
Borrowing Authority Act
district was involved there was a Congressman who was going to feel the direct impact of Canadian action.
The moral of the story is that a Government which can only see Americans as friends, instead of realizing the need to be businesslike and tough at times with them, will lose the opportunity to drive home to Americans that if they set out to hurt us, as happens in area after area, we may have to take action to hurt them in Michigan and other parts of the United States. I have yet to see that kind of toughness from this Government.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am delighted to join in the debate on Bill C-51, an Act to provide the Government with borrowing authority of $18 billion for the succeeding months and year. I am disappointed that there is no provision in Bill C-51 for the indexation of old age pensions next January 1.
Last weekend I had the opportunity to visit half a dozen communities in my constituency. In each community I was met by senior citizens who presented petitions to me to present to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Government. A senior citizen couple, both receiving Old Age Security pensions, will have their purchasing power decreased by $200. By 1990 they will lose approximately $1,200 of purchasing power per couple.
While I was in my constituency 1 received petitions from senior citizens groups in Little Current, Gore Bay, and Silver Water on Manitoulin Island. As well, I received a petition from the Senior Citizens' Club 455 in Espanola with several hundred names on it. It calls upon the Government to reinstate full indexation of the old age pension. In Elliot Lake 1 was presented with a petition by the President of the Senior Citizens' Group, Mr. Laverdiere. In each case the senior citizens groups make a very strong presentation for the Government to reinstate full indexation.
Perhaps the most poignant story was that of Mr. Ivan Bailey from Evansville who came to see me in my constituency clinic in Gore Bay. He told me of his situation, which 1 think is typical of so many senior citizen couples across the country. He told me that he was 76 years of age and that he and his family had been pioneers in western Manitoulin. His wife is partially disabled and he himself had a heart attack a couple of years ago. In spite of that, they are able to cope and live in their own home. He pointed out that they are very thrifty. For instance, he cuts his own wood and burns that rather than heating oil. They do not splurge in any way. He was simply asking why the Government is going to cut back on their old age pensions next January when they are struggling and working so hard to make it on their own.
I hope that the Government will amend Bill C-51 in Committee of the Whole and provide for full indexation of old age pensions. I think that is the only way in which the Government can correct the situation of the senior citizens of the country. It is not only senior citizens who are very concerned about the

June 17, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
deindexation of old age pensions. People who are from 55 to 60 years of age, many of whom have taken early retirement and are counting on the old age pension in order to have a certain level of purchasing power, are concerned as well. If deindexation goes through, over a period of five years a couple will lose $1,200 of purchasing power. Over a period of 10 years they will lose $2,000 or even $2,400 per couple. Someone who has made retirement plans based on receiving benefits of a certain level will not have the expected purchasing power in four or five years when he or she does retire.
There is very great concern about the authenticity of the commitment of the Prime Minister. Last year he called the indexation of old age pensions a sacred trust, saying that he would maintain it fully. Now that is being taken away. We want the Prime Minister to keep his commitment. He has indicated that he is waffling. I know that he is getting a lot of pressure from his caucus. I do not think he should wait until after the adjournment of the House a week from Friday to make that commitment. Senior citizens are very concerned about this cut-back and he should make his announcement in the next few days. Senior citizens of my constituency are sending in petitions which will be presented in the House. We will be making the strongest possible arguments that indexation of old age pensions should be maintained.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) was interviewed on CTV Question Period in April he indicated that he thought he could make cut-backs in a number of government programs and would not have to increase taxes. He seems to have changed his mind because many taxes will be increased for medium and low income families. This Budget does not provide much benefit for low income families. One of the concerns of senior citizens about the Budget is that at the same time as they will be losing $1.6 billion a year, a capital gains tax provision has been instituted which will cost the Government $1.25 billion per year within five years. If there must be a trade-off, surely senior citizens ought to be the beneficiaries rather than high income groups.
The Minister of Finance has indicated that he is not satisfied with the number of rich people in the country. Surely even the Minister of Finance would not wish to see people benefiting enriching themselves to the disadvantage of senior citizens. When this Bill goes to Committee of the Whole I hope the Government will back down on its plan to deindex old age pensions and reinstate the full benefits.
There are a number of other provisions of the Budget I want to mention because I believe that they all impact on this borrowing authority. Clearly, one sector which received no assistance from the Budget was the farming sector, except perhaps to help farmers get out of farming. Over the weekend, the Prime Minister said that his Budget was so popular that he thought he would be able to back down and give old age pensioners their full indexation. I hope he will do so very soon.
The budget provision of a capital gains tax exemption up to $500,000 allows those involved in agriculture to get out of
farming. That was a commitment made by the Tories during the election campaign although their commitment was to provide full capital gains tax exemption.
The agricultural community is clearly dissatisfied with the federal Budget. For instance, the board of directors and county presidents of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture met in Toronto on June 6. Their resolution states:
Whereas the federal Government has betrayed the farmers of Canada by presenting a Budget which totally ignored the results of its own consultative process and the commitments of the Government of Canada; and whereas the Government has not only ignored its own promises, it has ignored the legitimate needs of our farmers; therefore be it resolved that we are demanding that the Government live up to its own commitments made during and after the election campaign and that in order to get this message across to our Government, we recommend the following action-
They recommend that each MP from the Province of Ontario be petitioned by several members of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture and that the Ontario Federation and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture hold an executive meeting on June 19 to form a national action plan to bring the frustration and disenchantment of the agricultural community over the Budget to the attention of the Government.
Clearly the Budget strikes out at Canadian agriculture. For instance, the Government will impose a 9 cent per gallon tax on gasoline and farm fuels early in September of this year. Out west, where agriculture and the use of fuels is a major industry, they are terming this the "harvest tax". It is a tax on western Canadian farmers' harvest, imposed by the Tory Government. This will cost several hundred dollars, and perhaps more, on very large farms. The tax will increase once again in January when the 1 per cent sales tax is imposed on agriculture and all commodities in the country.
Last fall, the Government flamboyantly boasted about how it would reduce the tax on farm fuels. In fact, it is reimposing that tax this September, early in the harvest season. It is interesting to note that the Government was considerate enough of the tourist industry not to impose that tax during July and August, but it had no reservations whatsoever about imposing it just as harvest begins. For that reason western farmers are calling it the harvest tax.
Not only will the 1 per cent sales tax increase tax on farm fuels on January 1, it will be imposed on other agricultural input costs and production costs. Furthermore, a massive tax has been imposed on our tobacco farmers who have been suffering from changes in the personal lifestyle throughout the country. The Minister talked about some accommodation in that respect but no backing down. The wine growers in the Niagara escarpment and other areas of the country have expressed their concern about the 2 per cent excise tax on alcoholic beverages. Clearly, the Budget practically ignores agriculture.
The Government said that it would clarify Section 31. In fact, it did not do that in the Budget and has taken no action, although a committee report recommended that the limit of deductibility for off-farm expenses be increased from $5,000 to $10,000. There was a commitment during the election campaign as well as a recommendation by the Finance Committee
June 17, 1985

of the House to establish an agri-bond program providing money at 8 per cent interest. These would be long-term, low interest rates to assist some 39,000 farmers who are facing serious financial difficulty. There was no action on that agribond program.
Therefore, groups such as the Ontario Federation of Agriculture are planning an emergency meeting on June 19 to prepare a national action program to counter the lack of action by the federal Government in its Budget.
The Prime Minister stated at the First Ministers' meeting on the economy in Regina that no one has increased productivity and assisted the country more than agriculture in the past several years. People like Harry Pelissero, President of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, are now calling on the Prime Minister to explain why that sector is not recognized in the Budget if it has made such a great contribution to our economy.
One of the few areas singled out for cut-backs by the Nielsen committee is agriculture. Some $50 million a year will be cut from the Department of Agriculture. Although a number of programs will be severely cut back by the Government, it does not make it clear which ones. However, it is clear that the cut-backs will be $50 million this year, $50 million next year and $50 million the year after that.
The budget documents refer to programs like the dairy support program, agricultural commodity transportation and crop insurance as being subject to cut-backs. While it has not been made clear what will be cut back, we know that the Department of Agriculture is facing those cut-backs.
All of this is taking place when agriculture is under attack from beyond our borders as a result of the bungling of the Government. Last week, for instance, the United States Government imposed an even larger countervail duty of 5.5 cents a pound on our hogs and pork products going into the United States. That is a very substantial increase which will cost the hog producers of this country very dearly.
The Prime Minister met with the President of the United States in Quebec City. They were to solve all these problems in terms of trade with the United States. Clearly, these problems have been exacerbated in every realm. Whether it is steel, raspberries, pork or fish, our entire trade system with the United States, at a time when the Prime Minister talks extensively about improving trade relations, is incredibly worse. The support or bonus program on grain will drive down the international price of grains and have a devastating impact. Not only in North America, but in Europe and in other areas, the Government has clearly bungled our international trade relations. This is having a devastating impact upon our agricultural community, along with the lack of action in its Budget.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) raised a very important matter. I appreciate his question. He drew some similarities between the problems of fishermen in Atlantic Canada and the problems of farmers. Clearly there are some comparisons which can be made.
I should like to look at the quotas and countervail duties which have been imposed by the United States. In fact, last week it imposed a duty on fish from Atlantic Canada of approximately 20 per cent, while at the same time it imposed a countervail duty on our hogs of some 5.5 cents per pound. This is having a devastating impact on the price of hogs and has had such an impact since April 1 when the United States imposed it. We certainly see the similarity. There is sort of similarity in the approach of the United States, despite the comments of the Prime Minister about how he will improve trade relations.

June 17, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
1 cannot remember, in the 17 years I have been a Member of Parliament, so many duties, countervails and threats of countervails being imposed. They are all on our primary producers who are already faced with very low commodity prices, for example, fish, agricultural products and softwood lumber. I do not believe anyone in the House will remember such massive countervails and quota plans between Canada and the United States in the past. It is clear that the Government is messing up our entire relationship in terms of those products, all of which have been in very low price positions for the last while.
With regard to the Hon. Member's question concerning duplication of federal and provincial government programs, I doubt that there is that much duplication. For instance, if we look at crop insurance, the federal Government has put up half the premiums and the producers have put up the other half. In most cases the provincial Governments have administered the crop insurance program. It has been a very beneficial program. The Minister runs around the country proclaiming what he has done for farmers since last September 4. One figure he quotes is something like $530 million which has been paid out in crop insurance. That is an insurance program which the former Liberal Government put in place, into which producers pay. As well, the federal Government pays into a fund and the provincial Governments administer the program at a relatively small cost compared with the cost of the premiums for the program. If the Government is proposing that provincial Governments, as I understand it is doing, will put up a third of the cost, similar to the proposed tripartite red meat stabilization program, I think it will find a very cool reception. The reception on the part of provincial Governments having to put up as much as the federal Government will be about as cool as the reception of the deindexation of old age pensions on the part of Atlantic Premiers, all of whom are Conservatives. I do not think many provincial Governments are prepared to put up that additional money for the crop insurance program.
With regard to research and so on, it seems to me that the money spent on research and on developing new varieties of grain, fruit and vegetables, is really a reach toward the future. If we develop a grain which is more hardy or more resistant to disease or will produce greater yields by 5 per cent or 10 per cent, that is the price we pay to be successful five, ten or fifteen years down the road.
In the tripartite red meat stabilization hearings, we heard that provincial Governments in the Maritime Provinces really wanted to see feed freight assistance provided, whether it was provided through the stabilization program or through a direct feed freight assistance program. I do not think they want to see the Government cutting back on it. It seems to me that the Government should be providing a feed freight assistance program, while at the same time doing the necessary research and development to make Atlantic Canada self-sufficient in grain so that hog and beef production can continue there, even though in the initial drafting of the tripartite red meat stabilization program they may not be qualified.
So I think the Hon. Member has raised some very important points concerning the Government's attitude towards management, where it essentially wants to cut back on programs like agricultural assistance, feed freight assistance, grain inspection and crop insurance.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very interested in participating in this debate this morning and I want to get very quickly to the heart of my remarks because they relate to a very serious situation which has developed in my constituency. Usually I do not use the 20 minutes allotted to me to make a speech in this Chamber to speak on a local issue, but the subject of my speech today is a very serious one and it relates to job creation and the possible collapse of a major and historic industry, the former Cockshutt Plow Company, now called White Farm Equipment Canada Ltd. This firm goes back to the 1870s, so it is really a historic company with regard to the production of agricultural implements.
Bill C-51 is an Act to provide borrowing authority, and certainly there is nothing new or revolutionary about it. Usually Members of Parliament do not question the amounts of money involved because we all know that, particularly these days, it takes a lot of money to run a country. Governments run out of funds and they have to seek authority from this Chamber, Parliament, in order to borrow funds to keep payments going. However, we do use a Bill such as C-51 to question the Government's wisdom in spending that borrowed money. From time to time we put forward suggestions as to how we on this side of the House think the money should be spent. For example, in my opinion very often public funds are spent frivolously by this Government, and this is true of other Governments in the past.
We have the wife of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who has, so I understand, a spanking new office in the Langevin Building, and I question whether or not the taxpayers of this country should be paying for the operation of that office. It is my right to question that, and I do not know whether the money should be spent in that way. This certainly should be examined very thoroughly. Something else which might strike one as being very trivial but nonetheless symbolically important is whether public funds, even a few dollars, should be spent on a new presidential style podium for our present Prime Minister bearing a coat of arms not of a political Party, not of an office, but one that is symbolic or emblematic of our country. It is not a symbol of office, it is an emblem of Canada. If any person in this country should have the right to use that emblem, it is not the Prime Minister, it is the Governor General. I question the propriety of that use. In the former Prime Minister's household we used to question whether or not the taxpayers should pick up the tab for his and his family's food, and for the nanny or nannies, present and past. These are probably nit-picking examples but symbolically they represent our concern on this side of the House as to how this borrowed money is spent from time to time.
June 17, 1985

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: As well as on a car and chauffeur for the Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent).

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
We could, on the other hand, spend borrowed money to maintain pensions at a respectable level for seniors who built this country. We have gone into great detail on that issue on both sides of this House over the last few weeks. We could also borrow money to help keep Canadians from falling further and further into poverty. We could borrow funds to help preserve the quality and way of life for many other Canadians. We could use borrowed money to create meaningful jobs.
I have a modest proposal for the use of some of the borrowed money and, as I said at the outset, it has to do with a very serious financial and industrial problem in my constituency of Brant. This Government could offer to guarantee loans to White Farm Equipment Canada Ltd. in order to keep it from going under, thereby putting about 600 human beings out of work and on unemployment insurance. It would also take with it other smaller industries and suppliers, along with their employees, to say nothing of the hundreds of employees in the dealer network across the country. So we are talking about a very, very serious situation, one which I have raised on a number of occasions in the House and privately with the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens). I must say that he has been very accommodating and very positive, but so far no action has been taken. This would not cost the taxpayers one cent. Granted, the agricultural implement industry is going through tough marketing times. Harvesters or combines are certainly not in any great demand and the market is depressed. As my hon. friend from Algoma was saying a few moments ago, one reason for this is the deplorable state of finances in which our farmers find themselves at this time. The last Budget certainly did nothing to help that situation. Indeed, as the Hon. Member and others have pointed out, all that that Budget did was to make it easier for farmers to quit, give up and sell out. Well, that is a hell of a way to try to keep a basic major industry going in this country. What is happening to White Farm is the industrial spinoff from that kind of policy.
When I say this will not cost the taxpayers a cent of this borrowed money, I mean it. The money would only be in the form of a loan guarantee to tide this company over for a year, possibly two years, until, hopefully, the western agricultural market picks up, as well as that of central Canada. I call upon the Minister, then, to show some entrepreneurial spirit on the part of his Government and take a risk, as the former Government did. I would point out that as a result of the 1983 bail-out, so called, White Farm not only continued in production for two more years, but it increased its share of the Canadian combine market from 7 per cent to 22 per cent. The company is doing very nicely with a new Canadian owner, a president who is on the job in Brantford every day at his office, with a Canadian management team and a state of the art R and D facility, which was paid for in part by taxpayers' money over the years. The rug was pulled out from under the company, not because it was mismanaged or the market
Borrowing Authority Act
disappeared, but because of a foreign finance company, Borg-Warner, which decided, legally and quite properly, that it no longer wanted to have any of its money invested in White Farm Equipment Canada Ltd. The rug was pulled out at the very worst time. We cannot say that it was unfair on the part of Borg-Warner to do so. I suppose from its point of view, it was just good business. However, it dumped the whole financial problem back in the lap of White Farm Equipment of Canada.
For the first time in years, the profits that were being made at the Brantford facility were staying in Brantford. In the 1970s, when White Motor of Cleveland owned it, the Brantford facility made profits at a time when the market was buoyant. However, where did the money go? It was sucked out of Brantford to Ohio year after year. That was one of the things that lead to the financial problems of White Farm Equipment. When the recession hit in the early 1980s, it had no reserve capital. Furthermore, after the Cockshutt family sold out to foreign interests, virtually nothing was done to improve the plant or facility. There were virtually no capital expenditures at all. The only thing that was improved upon, updated or upgraded was the R and D facility which produced the state of the art axial-flow combining technology, and that facility would not have been built had it not been for the Canadian and provincial Governments which turned over a great deal of money to get that project launched.
Last week we did away with FIR A and brought in Investment Canada. We told Americans to come to Canada to buy us out. I have just given a perfect example not of why we should keep foreign money out but of why we should keep a very tight rein on how foreign investment in this country is used. It must always be used for the benefit first of this country and second of the foreign country or corporation.
Brantford is facing a very tense situation this morning. The deadline of the receivers, Peat Marwick, was arrived at last Friday at twelve o'clock. To the best of my knowledge, it has not been legally extended as Peat Marwick did not advertise an extension. So far, no word has come from the office of the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion regarding an extension. We are hanging in the balance right now and are waiting with bated breath.
We do not know whether or not White Farm Equipment will be alive tomorrow or whether or not those 600 men and women who work in the plant and office will have jobs. We do not know whether or not the Government has the courage to put up a loan guarantee of some $30 million in risk capital to save those 600 jobs at the plant plus several hundred other jobs in the dealer distributorships and supplier industries, and indeed to save several of those supplier industries.
We are only asking for $30 million in loan guarantees to save White Farm Equipment. That is not a great deal of money. It equals the approximate cost of giving away capital gains tax exemptions to about 50 of the wealthy friends of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). That is really what $30

June 17, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
million amounts to. It would preserve a way of life that began when the Cockshutt Plow Company opened its doors in 1877. At that time, it became a world renowned harvester company and its products were extremely popular in the Canadian West for many generations.
The recent history of White Farm Equipment is one of ups and downs, lay-offs and recalls, recessions and depressions. We saw interest rates choking off sales in 1981. We saw the recession hit both the farm community and urban Canada in 1981, 1982 and 1983. Some parts of Canada are still suffering from that recession. As I said earlier, we saw the former American owners siphon off profits in good times and then shut the plant down in tough times. We saw the American owners sell out when the times became so bad and the future so grim that it was not worth keeping the company. However, no one in Brantford really ever believed that Cockshutt, or White Farm Equipment as it is called today, would ever really disappear. They believed that it would survive somehow.
White Farm Equipment was not a leach industry. In 1983, it went to the provincial Tory Government and the federal Liberal Government to ask for loan guarantees to keep it going. As I said a few moments ago, it increased its share of the Canadian combine market from 7 per cent to 22 per cent during the toughest years experienced on the farm front in recent history. White Farm Equipment proved that it can produce a state of the art harvester like the axial-flow combine. It was all set to produce a new, smaller version of the 9,700 class harvester that would be more economical to operate and would sell at a lower price when Borg-Warner in the United States pulled the plug. Unfortunately, that could not have come at a worse time.
What can be done to rectify the situation? I suppose that what I am pleading for this morning is for the Minister to announce sometime today that there will be a loan guarantee forthcoming to White Farm Equipment because times are going to improve on the farm front. If they do not improve, we are going to go right out of the agricultural business altogether. If times get any worse, it will be the end of the agricultural sector, we will end up importing almost all our food and we will be paying world prices.
I think the Government had better put aside its ideologies for the time being and realize that there are some sectors in the Canadian economy in which the private enterprise system simply does not function at 100 per cent efficiency and cannot do so for a number of natural and normal reasons, perhaps unlike private enterprise in the United States. If the farm community needs assistance at this time, surely this is not the time to reduce aid to farmers by $50 million per year, but it is the time to increase aid to those who are just on the brink of going under.
In the newspaper, I read the other day that net farm incomes are supposedly up by 30 per cent this year. I cannot for the life of me understand that figure. My riding is often referred to as an urban riding, but it includes the entire county of Brant. Some of the best farmers and some of the ones that were the most prosperous in the past live in Brant, and are still
trying to hold on. Last week I spoke to some of those farmers. They were even more shocked than I was to read in the paper that net farm incomes were up by 30 per cent. Everyone to whom I spoke had a net farm income that was down.
As I said this morning, the Government, through its Budget, proposes to make it easier and financially more inviting for established farmers to sell and get out of the farm business. That will certainly not help the agricultural implement industry and it will certainly not help a community like Brantford, a community which has already been sorely hit by the recession of the early 1980s.
The community of Brantford is slowly climbing back to a better employment figure. There is still an unemployment rate of about 14 per cent in the City of Brantford. Even with the Summer Works Program, it will still be a very serious situation. Are we going to add another 600 and possibly another 200 unemployed to that list? I sincerely hope not.
What we are going to have to do is what the Government did in the case of Domtar. The Government is going to have to set aside its ideological strait-jacket for the moment and ask what is in the best interests of the public. It must ask itself what, apart from what is in the best interests of the company, is in the best interests of the public.
I urgently call upon the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, today, or at the earliest possible opportunity, to announce that the Government-as in the case of Domtar- will guarantee a loan of $30 million so that White Farm can continue until the market picks up, which should not be more than two or three years. The Conservative Government at Queens Park is prepared to give $10 million. There is private sector financing to the tune of approximately $5 million. However, another $30 million in loan guarantees is required.
I would also like to thank Members of Parliament of all Parties from southwestern Ontario who wrote letters of support, after receiving a letter from me which requested that support. I am not going to suggest what those Members recommended, but it was gratifying to know that they too are interested in maintaining those jobs.
I hope the Minister will consider every avenue and come forward today or tomorrow with a positive statement which will keep those 600 families out of poverty and put them back to work.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in order that I maintain the rules of relevancy, I will preface my remarks by saying that there is absolutely nothing in the Borrowing Authority Bill of $18 billion which will solve the problems that were created in the Budget which was tabled on May 23 by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson).

In the last six or seven days I have had the opportunity to travel widely throughout western Canada and parts of Ontario to ascertain firsthand the reaction of a number of groups in our society who have been affected adversely by the Budget. I was absolutely astonished to realize how little support the Government has for some of the measures in the Budget. I am surprised that members of the Conservative Party have been so silent throughout the debate which has taken place during the last two or three weeks in the House. I must admit, there are some rather courageous Conservative back-benchers who have had the conviction to stand and ask the Minister of Finance to reverse himself on some of the very unpopular measures which are in the Budget.
In addition, I note with some surprise, and I suppose with some contentment, that as a result of the Budget, the Conservative Party was forced to hold a special caucus in Ottawa this past weekend. Of course, I did not have the privilege to enter that room. Frankly, after witnessing the way in which the Conservative Party's blueprint for economic renewal was delivered on May 23, I can say that under no circumstances would any opposition Member even contemplate the idea of agreeing with it. I hope that the Members who attended the special caucus meeting at least had the courage to indicate their constituents' response and to give, Firsthand, their opinions on the ridiculous and unfair deindexation proposal which was made by the Minister of Finance. I am sure, within the confines of those four walls, that both the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) learned that there are the makings of a taxpayers' revolt against some of the measures in the Budget.
I see that the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) is in the House. I visited Saskatoon last week and met with hundreds of concerned senior citizens. They are concerned about the impact of deindexation, not only on Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement, but also about what will be the future intent of the Government on issues which affect the elderly and those in our society who are below the age of 65, who will be affected adversely by deindexation. Those people have no common voice to speak for them. I know that the senior citizens in Saskatchewan who represent those groups have repeatedly asked for the presence of their Conservative Members of Parliament to explain and convince them of the fairness of that tax measure. I suspect the reason for which those people have not seen Conservative back-benchers or front-benchers is that those Members are afraid to face the people who will be affected adversely by the Budget.
Where in the Borrowing Authority Bill are the funds which will reverse some of the direction which was in the economic blueprint of May 23? I have called the Budget a reverse Robin Hood budget. Not only does it take from the poor to give to the rich, the Budget will make the rich richer and the poor poorer. Any Conservative Member of Parliament who can stand before his constituents and attempt to justify the Budget as being fair and compassionate will require a good speech writer.
Borrowing Authority Act
It took approximately two weeks for the full impact of the measures to be understood by Canadians. They are now very much aware of exactly what is the full intent of the Government with respect to deindexation, not only as it pertains to senior citizens, but as it pertains to personal exemptions and the effect which that will have on middle-income Canadians.
Canadians will no longer be fooled by the rhetoric which was heard during the 10 day debate on the Budget. In those 10 days I heard Minister after Minister tell the House that they had the support of the senior citizen of Canada for the deindexation proposal. The Minister of Finance indicated that old people had said they were pleased that the Government had brought in deindexation. He said they were willing to do their bit to ensure that the federal deficit is reduced. They did not mind that the Government was taking $50 a month away from them and giving $2 billion in tax cuts to the multinationals. The Minister of Finance said that the senior citizens did not mind the fact that the rich would get richer. He said the senior citizens felt that it was their sincere pleasure, as people who live close to the poverty line, to ensure that the acute shortage of rich in Canada would be remedied by the Budget. He said they felt happy that they would make the rich today even richer, because they know what the rich can do for Canada.
I listened to the rationale behind the moves of the Government to increase the capital gains exemption to $500,000. In essence, the Government is taking money away from middle-income Canadians and the people who live close to the poverty line and it is adding $125,000 to the pockets of the rich people of the country. I am sure there is some support. However, I would have to stretch my imagination to contemplate which two Canadians might agree with the proposal. We now recognize the facts. The Government has no support for the measures which will take away from the poor and give to the rich. That is the reality.
I defy any Conservative back-bencher who has been back to his riding during the last 10 days to rise in his place and give me the names of the people and groups in this country who support these tax measures. I believe there are some rather compassionate Conservative Members of Parliament who are silent in the confines of this chamber, who have a great deal of concern about those people in our society who are below the age of 65. I am speaking about the widows in our constituencies who are between the ages of 60 and 64 years and whom you and I both know, Mr. Speaker, represent true hardship cases because there is no support system within our Governments, either provincial or federal, which represents their interests.
One thing I have learned in the last two weeks is that the New Horizons program which we instituted some six years or seven years ago was instrumental in creating a number of senior citizen groups and infrastructures across this country. It has allowed the senior citizens to form groups which can speak with one voice in representing their interests. However, there is

June 17, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
another group in our society which will be just as adversely impacted by this Budget but which does not have the infrastructure or the organizations to speak for it. There is no voice for the poor in our society who are below the age of 65 but whose needs are just as crucial. I can report to you, Mr. Speaker, that in my travels across the country last week, 1 found that every one of those senior citizen groups I spoke with in order to solicit their views on the Budget indicated to me that they are prepared to take up the challenge for those people under the age of 65 years who are going to be just as adversely impacted by this Budget. Thank heavens there are people in this society who have some compassion and some sense of justice.
When the Minister of Finance indicates he is prepared to have the burden of the deficit reduction taken out on the backs of the poor, it seems to me that the Conservative Party has a warped sense of justice. Now I understand why it was required in the Budget speech to put in the word "fair" 26 times. Members of the Conservative Party had to first convince themselves that the Budget was fair before they attempted to do their sales job on the people across this country. We as an Opposition Party have indicated that there is no support for the move of deindexation, the federal excise tax changes and gasoline tax increases. I would like to focus for one or two moments, Mr. Speaker, on these particular areas. We have had the impact of those taxes pushed through a computer model, just as the Minister of Finance had the opportunity to do before he put his budget to the Canadian public. I am sure that the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister of this country knew, when that Budget was tabled on the night of May 23, that as a result of deindexation, the increased federal excise tax and gasoline tax, another three-quarters of a million Canadians who are presently living just above the poverty line were going to be pushed below it over the next five years. Those figures have now been confirmed by the Canadian Council on Social Development.
When I put these questions to the Minister of Finance some 10 days ago, he had no quarrel with the numbers I presented to him. We see four or five days later in a report by Canadian Press that in fact, the Minister of Finance was aware. He had economic econometric models done which indicated that in fact three-quarters of a million additional Canadians would be pushed below the poverty line as a result of his budgetary measures.
I recognize that in the last 10 days we as an Opposition Party and the media have primarily focused our attention on the impact of deindexation on senior citizens. In the days ahead we will still push the Minister of Finance to reverse himself on his decision. The fact is that of those 750,000 persons who are going to be pushed below the poverty line,
230.000	persons will be senior citizens. That leaves another
520.000	Canadians who are below the age of 65 who will experience the same loss of roughly 20 per cent purchasing power, which will force the poor in our country to be poorer by 20 per cent. I find it incredible that the Conservative backbenchers have not risen in this House of Commons and asked
their own government front-bench to reverse itself on these issues which are affecting their constituents.
Surely you will understand, Mr. Speaker, because you come from the Province of Quebec, that there have been fluctuations in the unemployment rate there. There is not one Member of Parliament in this House of Commons who has a monopoly on poor people. There is not one Member of Parliament in this House who has a monopoly on senior citizens. In every one of our constituencies there are senior citizens who have been adversely impacted by this Budget. There are people in our constituencies who are poor by anyone's definition of poverty, including Statistics Canada. We all have those kinds of constituents in our ridings.
I feel very strongly, Mr. Speaker, that it is our duty as Members of Parliament to come to this forum and place before the front-bench opposite these questions so that people can fully understand the need for reversal of many parts of this Budget.
We are witnessing the anger of senior citizens toward the Government on these measures and, quite frankly, what I believe to be the snowballing effect of this anger so that the Government will have to reverse itself on the issues which affect senior citizens. Once that has been accomplished, whether that takes the next two weeks before the summer break or whether the Prime Minister will wait all summer to reverse himself, therefore bringing more political damage to the Conservative Party, there are still a number of other issues.
This is not a one-issue Budget. There is a smorgasbord of questions which have yet to be asked so that we can properly focus the attention of the Canadian public on the need for reversal in a number of other areas in the Budget. I really wonder, Mr. Speaker, if the intent of the Government is to arouse the Canadian taxpayers and make them so angry that there will be in essence a Canadian taxpayer revolt and a re-enactment of the Boston Tea Party. Is that the hidden agenda of the Conservative Party? If that is what it is waiting for, believe me it is going to come. If the Conservative Party believes that this issue is going to go away quietly over the summer, it is dead wrong. I can only say that in terms of philosophy, in terms of my sense of justice and compassion, this Government deserves to have the political fall-out and loss which will result from a Budget which creates wealth beyond comprehension for the select few. These capital gains provisions are going to cost the Canadian taxpayer more than all of the indexation which will affect the poor.

The number I have is $1.6 billion. Are we supposed to
June 17, 1985

worry about those people? It is a travesty of justice to make those nine families even richer than they are by taking the money from the poor who live in every one of our ridings across this country.
I was asked to check my figure and I stand to be corrected, Mr. Speaker. The capital gains tax provision will cost the Canadian taxpayer $1.25 billion-
