Mr. Speaker, I appreciated very much some of the comments made by the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith). However, there seems to be a state of selective amnesia among members of the Liberal Party with regard to the issue of deindexation of old age pensions.
The Conservatives have taken a measure which we find objectionable and which 2.5 million senior citizens find extremely intolerable. Their view has been echoed by children, grandchildren, and entire communities. On Friday night the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) was asked to defend this position in front of 1,000 women at the National Arts Centre. Never have I seen a Cabinet Minister as incoher-
Borrowing Authority Act
ent and incapable of defending an item of Government policy. She had just told the meeting that she herself had been very closely involved in the preparation of the Budget. If the junior Minister of Finance is not even prepared to defend this particular measure, it is obviously time for it to go.
I believe there were 130 or 150 Liberals sitting on that side of the House of Commons when Old Age Security was cut back by 5 or 6 per cent as a consequence of the six and five program. That was as cruel a blow to senior citizens in those days as what the Government is doing to senior citizens today.
I question why the Liberals can be a bit sanctimonious now. They are getting up to condemn what those who were in Government refused to say a word about at the time of the six and five program. Perhaps the Hon. Member could explain what has changed now, apart from the fact that he is in Opposition, to put him on the side of senior citizens today when he was not on their side two and a half or three years ago and did not at that time publicly break rank with the Government as he is urging Conservative Members of Parliament to do today.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, talk about a selective memory process. I will tell you the difference between Liberal compassion and Tory compassion. Under Liberal compassion, every person who lived below the poverty line or was on a Guaranteed Income Supplement received full indexation against the cost of living. It was as a result of the six and five program that we were able to break the psychological inflation barrier of double digit inflation. Does the Member really believe that today's inflation rate of less than 4 per cent came about as a result of Conservative economic policy instituted last fall? That began when the Liberal Government had the courage to witness the ravages of inflation on everyone in our society. We took a common front position.
Members of the Government front-bench who are now trying to defend their deindexation proposals should read in Hansard some of the comments they made at that time. How can they justify the fact that in their Budget of May 23 they did not have the decency to protect those who need help and protection in our society? There is not one iota of support for them. Their attitude is to let them eat cake and share in the burden of deficit reduction.
The Liberals did not do that. I am proud to be a Liberal because the Liberal Party understood what it was to be poor and underprivileged in our society, living below the poverty line as defined by Statistics Canada. Having understood what it was to be in those economic conditions, we fully protected those people in our society against the full CPI index.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on the Borrowing Authority Bill. I intend to make a speech about jobs; not possible jobs, nor jobs at some undefined date in the future, but real jobs now to help alleviate the suffering that is faced every day by the unemployed in the country.
This speech is also about fairness; not the kind of Tory fairness that gives pensioners and the poor tax increases while

June 17, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
the wealthy get more handouts, but real fairness which ensures that all Canadians contribute according to their ability, real fairness that does not benefit one Canadian at the expense of another.
This is also a speech about justice. It is not about Tory justice which can ignore line-ups at food banks or tell a miner in Atikokan who has not worked since the mines closed five years ago that he will have to wait for the private sector to find a job, but real justice which puts the welfare of people before the welfare of capital. It is about justice which realizes that we must stimulate job creation in the private sector, but also realizes that we must move immediately to create employment directly in order to ease the pain of poverty. As well, we must put an end to line-ups at food banks and restore dignity and hope to the 1.5 million Canadians who have been betrayed and ignored by the Conservative Government.
The Government had an option to say that it would live up to its election promises and the commitments it made to the unemployed, seniors, native people, young people, and women. Instead, it chose to wash its hands of its responsibilities and the trust placed in it. It says that job creation is up to the private sector.
We have seen great evidence of the trust that was placed in the Conservative Party last September 4. It is exemplified by headlines such as one appearing in the Thunder Bay Chronicle-Journal of Thursday, June 13, 1985, which reads, "Tories Robbing Poor", and one of June 10 which reads, "No Support for Deindexing". There is clearly a great movement in Canada. That is one thing I will give the Conservatives credit for. They have given senior citizens across the land the reason they have been looking for to unite, mobilize, and create a force which we have never seen before in the country and which will be around for a long time.
Something I learned as a community worker many years ago is that if you want to build a cohesiveness and pull people together, then threaten their basic existence. Developers do it all the time with their zoning applications and it seems as though the Government has copied its corporate friends.
Not only senior citizens but other Canadians are very concerned about what the Government has proposed. One seniors group in Thunder Bay, the Sunshine Club, has begun writing letters to their MPs, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). About 1,000 seniors in 15 clubs in Thunder Bay will be asked next week to join in an organization to lobby the Government of Canada strenuously.
Some individuals are already speaking up. An acquaintance, George Andrew-Cotter, a former City of Thunder Bay worker, is quoted in the paper as saying that widows are the ones who will be affected most. Widows have no other incomes. If they worked, it was in private homes or on farms. They have no other pension. He said that deindexation will hurt, not help the economy. Most of these people on Old Age Security spend all their pensions, and to reduce it reduces the amount of money
going back into the economy. He said, "there must be other ways of reducing the debt load without jumping on us seniors".
In Thunder Bay in 1981 there were approximately 11,327 people receiving government retirement income. About half of them received only the Old Age Security and the other half received Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement. That is an indication of the size of the group we are talking about in Thunder Bay, with a population of 120,000, who are angry.
Last Wednesday when my colleague, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) and I were travelling to our ridings to attend local functions, we discussed the growing movement in opposition to the government's Budget. We decided on Wednesday afternoon that we would give senior citizens in our ridings an opportunity to get together and express their frustration directly to us so that we could bring it back to the House and to the Conservative Party particularly.
I am pleased to announce that with 36 hours' notice, via the media, posters in buildings and by word of mouth, 225 senior citizens crammed into the Lakehead Labour Centre to voice their anger and outrage about what was contemplated to be done to them. They were not there just to talk; they were there to take action. They presented us with a number of petitions which, later today, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon and I will begin to introduce to the House.
They took more petitions to every corner of the community, to every senior citizens' building, to every church and corner store throughout Thunder Bay. Beginning today we will be presenting upwards of 1,500 signatures on petitions from all corners of northwestern Ontario; from Shebandowan, Kakabe-ka, Nolalu, Kaministikwia, Vickers Heights, Geraldton, Atikokan, Emo and Dryden. We will also be presenting petitions signed by delegates to the Manitoba-Northern Ontario District Command of the Royal Canadian Legion who held their annual conference in Thunder Bay last week. A number of them signed the petitions.
That organization also passed a resolution. They are representatives of the people who fought for freedom so that Canada could be the place it is today. They stated very clearly that they do not accept deindexation. We should remember that the Legion is an organization that tries to stay out of the political limelight. It wants to be seen as an organization serving its members. However, they recognize that in this instance they had to speak out because it is their members and their colleagues who are being affected by the Government's decision.
We also received a number of letters from individuals, a few of which I would like to read into the record. This is a letter from a retired businessperson in Thunder Bay, an individual who has been involved in the retail sector for some 30 years. He wrote to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp):
Dear Sir:
I confess I do not know whether to call you the "Right Honourable" or the "Honourable" Jake Epp, but since the budget was brought down, I assume it safe to omit the "Honourable" altogether.

You claim, sir, that we seniors support the budget. Here is one that does not. I contributed in my community as a small businessman and employer for 30 years.
I asked no government aid in business or providing my family's education. I was the exemplary taxpayer.
Now, sir, I face a dilemma. Your government has thrown out RHOSP. You have all but deindexed our pensions. Somehow the $500,000 capital gains exemption does not fit in with my financial plans. But how can anyone plan a future if they cannot trust the government? There is one thing I can do.
I have always voted Conservative, no more. I have been betrayed. Please tell Mr. Mulroney that here in Thunder Bay we don't like broken promises. We won't be fooled by deep toned double talk and we don't support your "tricky dickie" budget.
Another young individual from Atikokan wrote:
I would like to say a few words about the Conservative's plan to deindex pensions. I think it stinks.
I find it hard to believe that they can justify hitting our senior citizens with backwards punitive cuts, saying that it is time that the seniors did their part to help the country's economy. It seems to me that they already have.
The citizens which the Conservatives have chosen to rob have suffered the hardships and deprivations of recessions and depression, have fought in world wars to keep Canada a free country, and have worked all their lives to build a better place to live.
It is especially galling to see this substantial slashing of Senior Citizen's incomes when the Conservatives have decided, in the same budget, not to initiate their promised tax on the rich who manage to get away without paying any income tax. We are told that this tax would be complex and must be studied. Obviously the Conservatives feel it is easier to withhold from the Senior Citizens their rightful pension payments than to tax rich big wheels who might make waves or perhaps (how cynical) withhold political contributions.
The third letter regarding this subject comes from a gentleman I know well from the village of Vickers Heights, which is part of Thunder Bay. He writes:
My wife and I must heartedly protest the latest round of cuts especially to seniors.
Mr. Wilson in his latest budget is totally unfair to us the seniors of this great country. With the rise in the cost of living being a constant threat to our way of life, we must be indexed to the full amount of the cost of living. You should come down to our level and find out that it is tougher each year.
Further:
The latest federal budget has been a rather tough one for us that are retired.
It is not only individuals who are responding to the grounds well but editorials as well. Lakehead Living, an award winning weekly in Ontario, wrote in an editorial this past week:
There is an ironic twist to the federal government's recent budget. The government has produced a budget which puts further hardship on senior citizens and has released it just a few days before the proclamation of a month devoted to saying "thank you" to our senior citizens.
If the partial deindexing of the Canada Pension Plan was not such a blow to the income of our senior citizens the timing of the release of the budget, so close to Senior Citizen's month, would be laughable.
However, the deindexing of the pension system is a serious matter and is one that will take hundreds of dollars away from our seniors each year. That is money they cannot afford to lose.
Finance minister Michael Wilson's statement that seniors must share their portion of bringing down the national deficit is an insult to our elderly. Many of our senior citizens have already gone through one recession in the 1930's and have "shared" the burden of putting that economy on its feet. Mr. Wilson is very mistaken when he says seniors support his new budget. Opposition to deindexing is quickly gaining momentum among seniors across the country.
The Conservative government has awakened a potent political force in our senior citizens and if they are not careful they may pay for it in future elections.
Some would suggest that these are New Democratic senior citizens or that, heaven forbid, Lakehead Living is a New
Borrowing Authority Act
Democratic front. This is an issue which has stretched across all party lines.
In the public meeting which the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon and I held on Friday, we heard clear representations from every political party in the House and in the electoral system of Canada. I draw the attention of back-bench Members of the Conservative Party to the fact that they should not be afraid; they are not alone if they object to deindexation. For example, the Provincial Member for Fort William, a gentleman who took my place in the Ontario Legislature some eight years ago, attended our meeting to support senior citizens, wrote a letter to the Minister of Finance and ran a newspaper ad in the Thunder Bay newspapers which read: "Support Senior Citizens-Protest Deindexation of Old Age Pensions", in which he indicated that he strongly protested the deindexation of old age pensions and urged the federal Government to reconsider. He invited the constituents of Fort William and Port Arthur to write to him and that in turn he would forward them to the Minister of Finance, to let him know that not only New Democrats and Liberals but Conservatives objected to deindexation, this attack on our senior citizens.
The Government has awakened a giant, and it will regret it, not just today, not just tomorrow. Senior citizens, those who voted Conservative last September, did so with some unease. On one hand, they voted to get rid of the Liberal regime with which they were fed up. We can understand that. In many cases they went to the Conservatives because in those ridings they tended to be number two and they saw it as a way to get rid of the then Government. However, on the other hand, in the back of their minds they were thinking about other years and other Conservative Governments under which they had suffered; they suffered through four years and quickly turfed them out. The Government has rekindled that fear. It has confirmed their worst fears. 1 can assure the Government that they will not forget three years or four years from now.
Before turning to other aspects of the Budget, I want to wind up my comments on deindexation with an appeal. This is an appeal which I made to senior citizens in Thunder Bay on Friday when we talked about how one can get one's word to Ottawa, not only through petitions but by writing letters. I told them that their letters did not have to be long ones, that they had to be directed to the Prime Minister and read as follows: "Dear Brian: Deindexation stinks. Yours truly". 1 encourage senior citizens and all others across the nation to write to the Prime Minister in care of the House of Commons.
I should like to move on to other matters. The most significant line in the entire Budget suggests that the new direction for Canada's Government is to reward success rather than subsidize effort. We should think about that comment for a moment and what a dramatic shift it represents, not only in Canadian public policy but in terms of our view of the world. It used to be that in this country effort was important and that the role of the Government was to assist Canadians to further

June 17, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
develop the development of our culture and economy. That is no longer the case. They cannot come to the Government for help because they cannot find any, unless of course they have already made it and really do not need it, unless of course they are successful and can come to the Government for their rewards, their hand-outs. This view is callous and regressive. It is social Darwinism at its worst. It is a denial of all on which society is based.
Those words were echoed in a communique from a group which calls itself the Community Business and Professional Association of Canada and has as its motto "Fair Enterprise", an interesting approach. Its analysis of the federal Budget contains a number of important points which I would like to bring to the attention of the House. It indicates that the philosophy of rewarding success rather than subsidizing effort is very dangerous, in that it will curtail entrepreneurship in frontier areas of economic development. Risk taking is definitely discouraged in favour of classical endeavours. As indicated in the budget papers, the result will be that a greater number of profitable companies within each industrial sector will be taxable.
I see that my time is winding up. I have a number of other comments which I will reserve for another time, but in conclusion I should like to refer to how construction association representatives in Thunder Bay feel about the proposed 6 per cent sales tax on ready mix concrete and related building products:
We wish to register our most vigorous protest against the proposed imposition of this tax.
The construction industry (the country's largest single employer) has been devastated by the slowdown in the economy; registering unemployment in our area of up to 40 per cent. Investors need low interest rates and confidence in a stable construction climate, as stimulus to develop; not more taxes on the beleaguered construction industry and its suppliers to drive costs higher.
Our industry represents 15 per cent of the Gross National Product and 650,000 direct jobs, with an equal number in allied industries and professions.
The long-term effect this will leave on construction, and on employment in the construction trades is obvious.
At a time when the construction industry is at a low ebb, we must demand that these changes be rescinded.
Yours very truly,
Robert L. Irwin,
(Past President, Construction Association of Thunder Bay)
(Director, Ready Mixed Concrete Association of Ontario)
Whether it is senior citizens or business people, the Budget will not help them. It will hurt them. For that reason, we will not support the Government's financial plan.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words in this debate about pensions and also about another issue which may not relate directly to the Budget but certainly relates to the policies of the Government during the course of its First year in office. Of course I am referring to the question which was a key issue in my campaign in Ottawa Centre during the course of the election campaign last
summer, that is, to provide people who work in the Public Service of Canada the political rights which were promised them by the Conservatives when they campaigned for office.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Is that relevant?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Yes, it is relevant. Among other things, we are talking about 500,000 people who work for the Government of Canada, directly and indirectly, and are now deprived of their opportunity to protest the deindexation of pensions despite the fact that many of them will in fact be retiring shortly and will find themselves in a situation where the purchasing power of what they receive is gradually diminishing, thanks to the hard-hearted policy of the Government.
I cannot tell the House how concerned pensioners in my riding are about the Government's decision to deindex pensions. Some of the double-talk and gobbledegook which is coming from Cabinet Ministers and even from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is very confusing, to put it mildly. I always thought that when a measure was announced in the Budget, it had the force of law. In fact, it has been a tradition in Parliament that once a tax increase has been announced by the Minister of Finance, it takes effect immediately, despite the fact that it may take a number of months before the particular tax measure is translated into law. However, now we have the spectacle of the Government back-pedalling and trying to pretend that it really did not mean to do this to pensioners and, as a consequence, saying that of course it will monitor the situation, that it will not take place for several months, and that it was a proposal or an academic exercise.
If the Economic Council of Canada, the Business Council on National Issues or some other such body had come up with a series of proposals including the deindexing of pensions, it would have been appropriate for the Government to say that it would listen to the proposals with great interest. If a committee of the House of Commons had made suggestions for radical reform in terms of social security benefits or Old Age Security, again the Government of the day could have distanced itself from those particular proposals. However, we are now talking about a set of proposals contained in a Budget which took eight months to prepare and presumably set the course for the economic policy of the new Government over the life of its first term in office.
As I mentioned to the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith) a few minutes ago, I was struck by the fact that the other evening, the Hon. Member for St. Paul's, the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall), the junior Finance Minister, appeared in front of a meeting of 1,000 women in the National Arts Centre and when she, having worked with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on the Budget, was asked to defend the deindexing proposal, she did not know what to say.
The situation now is that virtually all Conservative Members of Parliament wish this proposal had not been made. They are distancing themselves to the point where the Minister of Finance is the only Member of Parliament adamantly in
June 17, 1985

favour of this proposal. I say to the Government it is about time it backed down and made sure that pensioners could sleep easily, knowing that their purchasing power was not going to be eroded because of a misguided proposal which should never have been brought forward and which should be withdrawn now. If Members opposite have made a mistake, be man and woman enough to admit it and withdraw the deindexing proposal now.
I think it is grossly wrong for the Government to decide it will double index the G1S but continue to take purchasing power away from senior citizens who happen to be just above the poverty line. I think that is the Government's intention, and I suspect if it acts at all, that is what we will hear, and I want to say in advance that it is wrong. Those pensioners who may be just above the poverty line right now are not very far above. In many cases in my riding, they still have to pay rent amounting to $400, $500 or $600 a month. If they are hanging on to their own homes, the average property tax for a home in Ottawa Centre is about $150 or $160 a month. The expenses of operating a home are rising rapidly and people in that situation cannot afford to see themselves lose $100 in purchasing power this year, $200 next year, $300 the year after and so on.
If the Government decides to restore indexing only to those who get the GIS, it will be doing by degrees what the Prime Minister said categorically the Government would not do when this issue was debated in Parliament in December. At that time he said universality was a sacred trust. It now appears he may decide to announce it is not a sacred trust anymore, but something to be eroded by 3 per cent per annum. This will go on until the present OAS is worth only 50 per cent of what it is worth today. For someone who is aged 50 and expects to retire at 65, the OAS will be virtually worthless and we will have what amounts to a means tested pension for the poor and nothing better. I think our country can do better than that.
I want to point out also that the other day the Senior Citizen Council of Ottawa-Carleton had a meeting. They represent all of the old people living in Ottawa-Carleton. They have some 60 affiliated organizations. They are strong, tough, bold, lively, and they said categorically that this cold-hearted proposal to reduce their inflation protection should be abandoned forthwith. While the NDP has been presenting petitions in this House for the last two and a half weeks, that organization has also been collecting petitions to see that this misguided proposal is withdrawn. They moved that copies of the resolution should be sent immediately to the Prime Minister and leaders of both opposition Parties, and they remind the people of Ottawa-Carleton that during the election campaign the Government said quite clearly that the PC Government would once more index the old age pension to the actual cost of living on a quarterly basis.
When they were in opposition, the Progressive Conservatives fought deindexing of the OAS. Now they are in Government, they suddenly find there are all kinds of reasons to take it away. Their excuses are just as hollow as the excuses of the Member from Sudbury when he tried to explain why the
Borrowing Authority Act
Liberals brought in six and five and cut back old age pensions by 6 per cent or so per annum.
The Council also pointed out that in the January 1985 Consultation Paper on Child and Elderly Benefits, the Government was again categorical in stating that in its view, no change was required in the OAS-GIS payment system. What was the Minister of Finance doing at that time? Did he sit in Cabinet when this question was discussed and the paper was reviewed and say he was going to get them in two and a half months, but he was not going to say what he was going to do right then? Was he refusing to play squarely and deal fairly with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), or was that Minister being duplicitous in publishing a consultation paper which he probably knew was going to be changed or violated in a very short time?
I think it is about time the Government stuck to its promises on this issue. We have seen a lot of broken promises and as far as our senior citizens are concerned, if 1 had a set of priorities regarding which promises to break, it would be to not break any at all, but if the Government is determined it is going to break its word, for God's sake, don't break your word to those senior citizens who contributed so much to our country.
A week ago today, at about this time, I was out on the steps of Parliament Hill when a number of people arrived to commemorate the fiftieth anniversary of the great trek to Ottawa which was broken up in Regina with tragic results by a previous Progressive Conservative Government. Some pensioners came to me and said "We want you to know that during the Depression we worked for 20 cents a day. We lived in the camps. There was no radio, no newspaper. It was like a concentration camp, or just about." They tried to break out but they could not. They lived in abject poverty year after year. They said "Now the country is prosperous and look what they are doing to us today." They asked me to please pass that message on to Mr. Mulroney and Members of the Government, and I am doing that right now.
The Government seems to have a passion for deindexing. It seems to have bought the gospel according to Colin Brown and the National Citizens Coalition right down the line. The Government is wrong on this issue, and I want to suggest that it is also wrong on deindexing pensions of people who work now or who have worked for the Public Service of Canada.
Last Friday I had a chance to meet with representatives of the Union of Economists and Statisticians. We talked about the Government's deindexation proposal which had been announced in conjunction with representatives of the PSA but quickly abandoned because it was clear that the Alliance spokespeople perhaps had made some mistakes. Certainly they did not understand what the Government understood they were getting. Public Service pensioners paid for indexing. They pay about the highest proportion of income for their pension benefit plan of any group of workers in Canada.
The actuarial assumptions the Government is using to try and back away from its commitments to indexing of Public Service pensions are hollow, unfounded, and have a great deal to do with the fact that for many years the earnings of the
5826

June 17, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
Public Service pension fund have been grossly below those that private sector pension plans were getting in the private market, or had it been able to get the benefit of interest rates available on long-term Government bonds. It looks as though the Government is trying to send this matter back to the advisory committee on pensions which has already dealt with it once and made recommendations which effectively amount to deindexing. You can hardly expect a group which has come up with one lousy proposal to turn around and give a better proposal the second time.
Therefore, I want to echo the concerns of many people in the Public Service or retirees and say that I for one, and my Party as well, would support the matter of Public Service pension plans being referred to a parliamentary all-Party committee which can get objective advice and make some objective recommendations. I think it would be grossly wrong to refer this to an in-House advisory committee which did a bad job last time, which perhaps badly advised the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret). This in turn led to an unfortunate rift between the President of the Treasury Board and the leaders of the major Public Service unions over something which in my opinion should never be implemented.
Public Service employees to whom 1 have spoken indicate quite clearly that if what they contribute is not sufficient to continue to pay for full indexation of their pension plans, they are prepared to look at a change in contribution rates. However, all of the actuarial calculations they have made indicate that what they are paying now is ample to maintain that indexation, particularly if they were to stop playing games by joining together the basic superannuation fund and the supplementary fund which has been created for indexation. That should be done, but if it is not done directly, I suggest that it be done by means of a review by a parliamentary committee.
I would like to conclude my remarks by speaking on the question of political rights. I do so in sorrow and with regret. During the election campaign, the Progressive Conservative Party promised, as did the NDP to provide full political rights for people working for the Public Service of Canada. I fought and won the election in the riding of Ottawa Centre on that particular issue and I am pledged over the life of this Parliament to do everything I can to make sure that those Public Service employees who deserve to get political rights do get them.
I believe that the President of the Treasury Board has been acting in good faith in terms of the discussions that he has initiated. I think, however, that he is being undermined by the Public Service Commission, which has been carrying out a holy war in favour of maintaining the present restrictions and by a number of senior mandarins at the Deputy Minister and Assistant Deputy Minister levels who believe that the present system should stay because it is necessary that a very small proportion of people working for the Public Service be untainted, pristine and seem to be non partisan. Most everyone to whom 1 have spoken agree that keeping a small proportion of
the Public Service in a state of political virginity is probably not a bad idea, but that should not apply to the 250,000 others who work for the Public Service of Canada, yet that is the position being taken by those who I believe are stoutly resisting the efforts of the President of the Treasury Board to implement the promise the Government made last fall.
I must say with regret that last week 1 held a press conference to announce that the court case which I initiated in conjunction with a number of members of the Public Service Alliance who are federal Government employees will go forward. We expect and hope to get a date before the Federal Court of Canada early in the fall. The lawyers are now getting together to resolve the subsidiary and minor issues so that the case can focus on the constitutional questions of the denial of fundamental rights of freedom of speech and association to people working for the Public Service because of the current restrictions in the Public Service Employment Act. That case will go forward because I felt I had no choice. After 10 months of a PC Government, the Government mandate is beginning to weaken a bit. The Government is having some set-backs in areas like pensions and there is a grave danger that it will forget this promise the way it has forgotten so many other promises it made to pensioners, public service employees and ordinary Canadians.
We have seen during the course of the elections held in the Yukon and Ontario that the situation facing people who work for the Public Service has not changed one tittle since the election. Members of the Public Service of Canada are no more free today than they were during the election campaign leading up to the September 4 election. They can give money, they can go to political meetings, they can hold membership in a political Party but they can do more. If a member of the Public Service of Canada were to have knocked on doors for a political candidate in the Ontario election, he or she would have run the risk of losing his or her job as a consequence. That is how serious the situation is, and no change has taken place.
I thought that the Treasury Board might have issued instructions to personnel officers in different departments indicating that it is doing its best to implement these changes and asking the personnel departments to inform those people who are members of bargaining units that it is okay for them to take part in election campaigns while keeping a low profile but that if they want to be campaign managers or candidates, of course the normal rules will apply. However, no such compromise was reached. In the meantime, the Public Service Commission has continued, in its status as an independent Commission reporting to Parliament, to give advice to the people who run the Public Service in the various departments to say that it is an offence to take part in elections. To reiterate the guidelines issued in the spring of last year, they effectively say that any action by anyone in the Public Service that might give the least cause to think that a Public Service employee is not impartial is suspect and should not be engaged in.
A few weeks ago when he appeared before the committee, the President of the Public Service Commission made public a
June 17, 1985

poll on political rights that had been carried out by Carleton University. That poll indicated that 30 per cent of the people working for the Public Service of Canada would in fact exercise more political rights if they were granted them through legislative action. I think that the President of the Public Service Commission was taking the view that that proved that most members of the Public Service do not want to have political rights. I say that when 80,000 people are saying that their fundamental rights are being denied them, something is wrong.
I think all of us know how small of a proportion of the general population is in fact politically active. Perhaps 2 per cent or 3 per cent of the population of Canada, during the course of an election year, goes to a political meeting or takes part in a political campgaign. If 30 per cent of the Public Service indicates tha they would like to be politically active, that is a very major proportion. I would say that if only 1 per cent said that their fundamental rights were being denied, something would be seriously wrong.
The Charter of Rights says that everybody enjoys freedom of speech, and that does not include an exemption with respect ot all people working for the Public Service of Canada. The Charter of Rights guarantees fundamental democratic rights to everybody and does not exempt people working for the Public Service of Canada. The Charter of Rights provides for freedom of association and does not except people who work for the Government of Canada but wish to take part in the activities of a political Party.
The Government has time before we adjourn on June 28 to make its intentions clear. I look forward to a statement by the President of the Treasury Board because for Public Service employees, this issue is just as important as the issue of pension rights and deindexation is for the two and one-half million senior citizens who have been so cruelly treated by this Government.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome this opportunity to speak to Bill C-51, but I would like to start by refreshing the memory of the public and explain that this is a very important piece of legislation which authorizes the Government to borrow an amount not exceeding 18 billion 200 million dollars for its operations, or as it says here: "... as may be required for public works and general purposes." In fact, this also means that when speaking to this Bill, Members are allowed to comment on a variety of subjects.
Mr. Speaker, if we look at the Government's strategy we are tempted to ask: Where is this Government going? Or if you prefer: What is their strategy? Actually, during the past nine months, we have seen the politics of style, the strategy of style, an attempt to sell a large Cabinet with a new Prime Minister-and I must say that on occasion, the Prime Minister and
Borrowing Authority Act
his Cabinet have cut a dashing figure on television-but that is not the primary responsibility of Government. It must be consistent and serious, and it is imperative that this Government firmly establish its policies both in the economic and social sphere. So at last we had a Budget, on May 23. We discussed this Budget for several days, and now we are considering this particular Bill which is aimed at authorizing the Government to borrow $18.2 billion. Billion, Mr. Speaker! Recently, someone asked me, and I was talking to high school students: what is a billion? So I said it was 1,000 million, and to try and put it into more concrete terms, I told them that to spend a billion, you would have to spend $1,000 every day for
3,000	years. They were speechless. I said yes. And of course $18 billion means you would have to spend $18,000 every day for 3,000 years.
So we cannot think in those terms. It is an incredible amount of money. It is a lot of money, and because this is a wealthy country, we have very big budgets.
Mr. Speaker, the Government is trying desperately to sell its budget. It is trying to save face by saying that the Budget has been well received. It should realize, however, that it contains a major defiency, which we have pointed out, and that is the proposal to de-index Old Age Security pensions. This is how the whole discussion on the Budget started, because we realized that in the figures we were given, the Government indicated the scope and the size of the Budget measures it was proposing.
The Government is desperately trying to sell the Budget to Canadians because, in my view, not many Canadians want to buy it. Conservatives have realized that the country is not willing to accept a Budget which will put the highest burden on those who are least able to carry it-the poor, the elderly and the unemployed. In his attempt to sell the Budget to Canadians, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), in a recent speech to The Empire Club of Canada in Toronto, said that the Tory Budget upholds public morality. Obviously, the Conservative Government distorts the understanding of the word "morality".
In its Budget, the Government has partially deindexed Old Age Security pensions. I have a document from the Department of Finance, released after the Budget, which indicates the effects of the various budgetary measures up to 1990-91. The document indicates that the deindexation of senior citizen's pensions will have an impact of $1.6 billion by 1990-91. The document outlines the revenue and expenditure impact of budget measures by national accounts component. The third column of the document from the Department of Finance was not made pulic. The first two columns which dealt with 1985-86 and 1986-87 were made public, but 1990-91 was not.
I would like to return to Old Age Security. That will have an impact on the deficit. Reductions in other fields of taxation, such as the modified indexing of personal income tax and the

June 17, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
personal surtax, the RHOSP and the child exemption will also have an impact on the deficit. The disability deduction has gone from minus-$15 million to minus-$50 million. Capital gains tax will cost the taxpayers of Canada S300 million this year, $600 million in 1986-87 and $1.2 billion in 1990-91. Canadians have a $500,000 capital gains exemption which will allow a $10,000 exemption this year and which will gradually increase over the next few years. They will be allowed to use those capital gains as a tax shelter.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: It is not a tax shelter.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Yes, it is a tax shelter. No tax will be applied to the capital gains which people realize, whether it is realized on a Kentucky horse, a condominium in Miami, paintings or jewels. In that $500,000 capital gains exemption, we would have liked to have seen some encouragement for jobs, small enterprises and research and development. In other words, the Government should insist that the money be used for the benefit of Canadians in Canada.
The tax treatment of pensions will mean a reduction of $235 million by 1990-91. Housing loans will be reduced by $45 million by 1990-91. The document lists other examples. For example, the freezing of unemployment insurance premiums will provide a reduction in the deficit of $10 million. I could list all the financial consequences of the Budget, but the one measure with which all Canadians are preoccupied is the measure which deals with the partial deindexation of Old Age Security. Child benefits will also be changed, including the family allowances. Tax exemptions for dependent children will mean a net reduction of $600 million by 1990-91. The families of Canada will say that is immoral. I cannot blame them.
By 1990 the Government will have cut social programs by more than $2 billion a year. That money will not be redistributed to needy Canadians-the old, the poor and the unemployed. It is another election promise which has been broken by the Government. It says it will use the money to reduce the deficit, although it promised that it would not do that. That is immoral. The 1.4 million unemployed Canadians say that it is immoral.
The Government will probably come to its senses in the next few days and change its mind on the question of the Old Age Security pension. I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will have the guts to come into the House and say that the Government has made a mistake and that it will not proceed in January 1986 with the Ways and Means motions which are necessary to implement the measure.
Mr. Speaker, the last time the Government asked the House to approve borrowing authority legislation, the circumstances were, of course, quite different. Hon. Members will recall that at the time, there had been no Budget, and we were being asked to provide borrowing authority for an amount that was far in excess of projected spending. The Government wanted to
borrow more than it had said it was going to spend. Obviously, we objected to that. This caused quite an upheaval in Parliament which went on for several months, until last December, when the Bill was passed because the Government, which was involved in a debate on universality at the time, wanted to reach agreement at any price before Christmas, and since time was running out in two instances, namely for the borrowing authority which it needed and which was essential, and there was also the debate on universality which was becoming an embarrassment, the Government set aside the last day of the session before Christmas for a debate on universality, in exchange for the Opposition's consent on the borrowing authority legislation.
Subsequently, the Senate or perhaps I should say the other place, Mr. Speaker, made a fuss, and this caused a number of problems that were perhaps more a matter of image than substance. The situation today with respect to Bill C-51 is different. The Government has brought down a formal Budget and tabled its Estimates. But there is another difference, and that is because the Government is asking for $18.2 billion to finance its extravagant gifts to the multi-national oil companies and rich investors, while at the same time it is telling the elderly they will have to tighten their belts. They were unable to set aside any part of the $18.2 billion to provide for full indexation of the Old Age Security pension for Canadians. That is the difference, that is what is so immoral and that it is why it is wrong.
Mr Speaker, what we are considering today is the morality of the situation. Is there any moral justification for telling
200,000	senior citizens that they will become poor? Because that is what the result will be, Mr. Speaker. Between now and 1990, this measure will put 200,000 Canadians below the poverty line. The immorality of this Government's request in the Bill before the House today prompts me to dwell a little longer on the Budget brought down on May 23 of this year, since as I said before, the Government's request is closely linked to the Budget. What the Government is suggesting, Mr. Speaker, is a single, primary and very narrowly-based objective. The purpose of the Budget is to bring down the deficit, so the deficit comes first and nothing is going to stop that.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think any Member in this House is against bringing down the deficit. It is a very worthy goal, and it is very important. But it must be done without putting the burden on the wrong people. What the Tories have done is regressive and unfair. They are well aware of that. Why put a tremendous tax burden on the consumer while giving big corporations and wealthy individuals special privileges? Why not be a little more flexible and allow more generously for job creation? Why did they cut $78 million from the Budget for training, development, and especially manpower training? Mr. Speaker, there is a very real possibility that all these measures will reduce purchasing power and with all these tax increases,
June 17, 1985

the situation is not going to improve, and it may well get worse later on.
Let us look at the figures, Mr. Speaker. These are not my figures, they appear in the Government's Fiscal Plan, a document given to us along with the May 23 Budget. In 1987 middle-income consumers will have to pay $2.4 billion in additional taxes, while at the same time about $540 million in benefits will be given to the companies that are so friendly with this Government. We know them. And the figures keep increasing, Mr. Speaker, to the extent that the business community will have a field day by 1990, while elderly and ordinary Canadians will have to make do with ever diminishing assistance.
Mr. Speaker, the social planning council recently published a very interesting document indicating:

"Summary of Major Budget Measures", and these are not my figures, these are the figures of the Canadian Council on Social Development. These are the costs, and I will repeat them again because it is extremely important for Canadians to know them. For example, Mr. Speaker, the Budget will decrease the buying power of a typical family with two children by more than $1,000 in 1990. By deindexing tax systems, by capital gains exemptions, it lowers the revenues of the Government of Canada which results in increased taxation on consumers. The increased pension contributions will be lower. It will eliminate the federal tax reductions, reduce the child benefit systems and reduce old age security. By 1990, Mr. Speaker, $2 billion will be cut from provincial Governments for post-secondary education.
I really would have liked to continue my remarks for the next half hour because I still have notes. However, Mr. Speaker, I would just remind Hon. Members that on voting on Bill C-51, they are voting on $18.2 billion. That is a lot of money and, for God's sake, let us put it where it should be, that is to help the aged, the poor and the unemployed.

subtopic: CALL FOR REINSTATEMENT
CALL FOR REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, how much longer are are we going to tolerate the mollycoddling of murderers who have been convicted of deliberately planning and killing one or more human beings? We put them in prison for 20 years and, during that time, we provide extra protection for them. They have security, and are given far better food than hundreds of decent, law-abiding citizens can afford.
They are entertained and taken to sporting events. Hundreds of our taxpayers' dollars are spent for pool tables and equipment, and periodically they may have their spouse or common law partner as a guest in a government trailer. All of this, of course, is with the compliments of the Canadian
taxpayer. We put the lives of prison guards on the line while they are with these murderers.
What about those who were murdered; young girls, young boys, women, police officers, and prison guards, many of whom were tortured and physically and sexually abused before their lives were snuffed out? Their bodies lie in the cold earth, with only relatives and friends visiting their graves. The loved ones left behind are the forgotten people of our nation.
"It would be barbaric to execute these murderers'', the bleeding hearts cry. They ignore such barbarism as molesting and then murdering a four year old boy, or the agony suffered by a teenage girl before her body was raped and burned, or the pain of forcing policemen to dig their own graves before being slaughtered. A majority of Canadians want such murderers executed. I grieve and weep for the murdered and their loved ones, not for the murderers.

subtopic: ETHIOPIAN FAMINE-WORLD UNIVERSITY SERVICE OF CANADA'S ADOPT-A-VILLAGE PROGRAM
ETHIOPIAN FAMINE-WORLD UNIVERSITY SERVICE OF CANADA'S ADOPT-A-VILLAGE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the International Year of Youth it is most gratifying to see the
major role the World University Service of Canada is playing in relief to Ethiopia. Its Adopt-a-village concept is unique and thrilling. Several cities in Canada have adopted a village in Ethiopia.
Toronto has adopted the village of Gode. Gode is located in the Agadon desert of southeastern Ethiopia. The Agadon has been suffering from a three-year drought wihch has devasted crops and depleted all water supplies. There is malnutrition, starvation, and other diseases associated with poor nutrition. There are already 300,000 displaced persons who are seeking food and water, and Canadian and Ethiopian relief workers expect the total to rise to over 1 million by the end of this year.
There are real practical needs. Two 10-tonne trucks, a mobile medical unit, medical supplies, water storage facilities, and more personnel are urgently needed. The cost is $450,000, and I urge all residents of Metro Toronto and other Canadians to support the Adopt-a-Village concept developed by the World University Service of Canada.

subtopic: OTTAWA CONFERENCE-WORLD-WIDE BENEFIT
OTTAWA CONFERENCE-WORLD-WIDE BENEFIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one of the Members of Parliament who is privileged to be attached to the delegation to the World Conference on Human Rights, I would like to say a word of congratulations to Ambassador Jay and all the officials of the Department of External Affairs who have formed the Canadian mission at that important conference. They have performed with a professional commitment worthy of the best traditions of the Canadian diplomatic corps.
Many people wonder, however, if it has been worth the effort. When the conference adjourns today and the delegates go home, it is feared that they may go home with little more than a communique phrased in diplomatic generalities and with a few rhetorical flourishes. Blacks can still be gassed at a peaceful demonstration in South Africa. Dissidents can still find penal servitude their reward for even a whisper of criticism behind the Iron Curtain.
But there is one gain from the conference. It is the recognition that if nations of the world can come together to discuss human rights within the borders of each other's countries, then human rights are not simply an internal matter anywhere. Human rights belong to everyone and they are a world responsibility that commands the concern of us all, not as citizens of one country intruding into the affairs of another, but as men and women who are sharing with others in their sufferings because we share a common humanity.

June 17, 1985

subtopic: GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS
GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the appointment of Jim Wood, a former RCMP corporal, to the Canadian Pension Commission at a salary of up to $65,000 has given further evidence of the Solicitor General's (Mr. MacKay) tendency to assist his friends at the expense of his official responsibilities. During the 1970s Mr. Wood was responsible for leaking confidential information on RCMP activities to the Hon. Member for Central Nova, now the Solicitor General.
This was in total violation of the oath of secrecy that Mr. Woods swore when he entered the force. By arranging for his friend, Jim, to receive this appointment, the Solicitor General has debased the RCMP oath of secrecy. He has sent a message to members of the force that they can violate their oath with impunity. Indeed, if they violate their oath for the greater glory of the Tory Party, they may even be rewarded.
Ironically, the details of Mr. Wood's appointment come at a time when the RCMP Commissioner is attempting to restore respect for the oath of secrecy within the force. Commissioner Simmonds stated in the Hatfield report that the value of the oath is "in setting a standard of professionalism and integrity that will assure public confidence and trust in the force. When the standards are not maintained, there is a consequential lessening of respect for the organization".
The Solicitor General is like a wrecking ball in his own Ministry. He should resign, and the Wood appointment should be rescinded.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government is asking the House for the approval of Bill C-51. 1 ask the House to consider how it can give its approval to such a Bill when the Government has betrayed elderly Canadians in its May 23 federal Budget. The Budget attacks the well-being of millions of elderly Canadians living on fixed incomes by increasing the cost of living for senior citizens through hidden and regressive taxes, while moving directly to cut the purchasing power of the Old Age Security pension.
Over the last few days, the Government, facing the understandable fury of millions of elderly Canadians and millions of Canadians generally about what it intends to do in its Budget, is hinting that it might be backing down on what it has said it would do when it comes to cutting purchasing power by deindexing the Old Age Security pension. Whatever the Government ultimately does, I do not believe that senior Canadians or Canadians generally should ever forget what the Conservative Government fully intended to do and may well still do in the Budget it presented to the House on May 23.
What were the promises made to elderly Canadians and later broken by the Conservative Government? On July 26, 1984, during the election campaign, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), speaking in Sherbrooke, Quebec, tried to create the impression that the Progressive Conservative Party would actually increase pension benefits for Canadians. He said, "We are committed to full pension fund reform to eliminate poverty among retired Canadians and to improve their standard of living".
In January this year, after the Conservative Government was able to examine fully the books of the Government and its financial requirements now and into the future, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) issued a consultation paper on benefits for the elderly and for children. The Conservative Government set out a number of principles in that paper which were to be considered as firm commitments. Let me quote the key principles. "Any savings which may result from program changes will not be applied to a reduction of the deficit". Second, "It should be stated at the outset that the Government regards the present system as a good one, which is working well". Third, "Changes in these programs which may
June 17, 1985

result from this review should improve benefits for those in need".
The final principle states:
Any net savings which may then remain, whether resulting from reductions in expenditures or additional revenues, should be applied to other priority concerns in the social affairs envelope. No such savings should be transferred to deficit reduction.
These are direct quotes from the paper that was issued on behalf of the Conservative Government in January of this year. The record of the Budget shows how far the Government has broken the commitment in that consultation paper.
Having outlined the basic principles that I have quoted in the consultation paper, we can see how the Conservative Government moved all too quickly in its Budget to try to fool Canadians into believing that it was acting to maintain the basic principles of protecting the well-being of elderly Canadians.
The Budget Speech delivered by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) devotes only four lines to state that old age pensions are being deindexed. That is to say, its purchasing power is to be reduced in perpetuity for all increases in inflation below 3 per cent, but indexation would remain for the Guaranteed Income Supplement.
Although the Conservatives try to show that indexing the Guaranteed Income Supplement makes up for deindexing or cutting the purchasing power of the Old Age Security pension, the fact is that continuing indexing of the Guaranteed Income Supplement protects only the purchasing power of that supplement. It does nothing to protect the purchasing power of the Old Age Security pension which represents at least half of the pension income of those elderly Canadians whose incomes are so low that they receive both the old age pension and the Guaranteed Income Supplement.
This Budget is deceptive and sneaky, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) put it, because nowhere in the Budget Speech is there an explanation of the true ramifications of deindexing. There are no concrete examples of how incomes of senior citizens would be affected by what the Budget-therefore the Conservative Government-fully intended and likely still intends to do. Through its broken promises and deception, the Conservative Government is betraying our senior citizens. The Conservative Government promised in its January consultation paper that no savings or additional revenues in the area of social programs would be applied to reducing the deficit but would actually be applied to increasing benefits. However, that commitment to elderly Canadians was betrayed in the Budget, and the confirmation of that betrayal was given on May 24 in the House when the Minister of Finance stated, "Everyone has been asked to share a little of the burden in order to get the budget deficit and the accumulating debt problem under control".
Last weekend in my community of Windsor I talked to many people. Many were senior citizens who asked me why the Government is expecting them to bear any burden of deficit reduction. They asked, "why does the Government believe that we are as well equipped as wealthy Canadians to
Borrowing Authority Act
bear any part of such a burden, if that is required? They said to me, "We have already made our sacrifice for this country. We have survived a depression and the Second World War and the post-war period." They said, "We have paid our dues. We have made our sacrifices. If there is a need for deficit reduction", they told me, "that burden certainly should fall on people much better off than us".
In January the Government told elderly Canadians that it regards the present system as a good one, one which is working well. It said that it is a sound system, one which should not be disturbed, and that changes in these programs which may result from this review should improve benefits for those in need. It said that savings should not be transferred to deficit reduction. However, the Conservative Government totally reversed itself on this by attacking the income and well-being of elderly Canadians for years to come, in perpetuity.
The reality is that the Conservative Budget is punishing middle and lower-income Canadians but is especially cruel to the elderly.
Figures developed by reputable bodies-not only a very reputable body like the Official Opposition-show that the four lines devoted to the elderly in the Budget of the Minister of Finance failed to note certain facts. First, as a result of the Budget, the real income of an elderly couple will fall nearly $1,200 by 1990. By 1995, the real income of an elderly couple will be cut by almost $2,600. The real income of elderly singles, mostly women, will be cut by $560 in 1990. By 1995, the real income of elderly singles will be cut by almost $1,300. Only Conservatives would believe that our senior citizens could afford cuts of this magnitude. Elderly Canadians, as well as all Canadians in general, will have to pay sales tax increases for gasoline, health care products, pet food, shampoo and other goods, which will amount to hundreds of dollars per year in lost income.
These facts represent the truth which the Conservative Government failed to tell Canadians in its Budget. These facts expose the broken promises and the deception of the Conservative Government in its Budget. The Conservative Government did not tell Canadians that its Budget would increase poverty. The Budget provisions introduced on May 23 will see more than three-quarters of a million Canadians fall below the poverty line by 1990, and more than 200,000 more elderly Canadians living on fixed incomes will be forced into poverty. The Conservative Budget will cast more Canadians into poverty than the global economic recession in 1981-82. All the assurances and commitments given by the Conservative Government were exposed as being empty and meaningless. In fact, they were replaced in the the Budget by what I believe to be a long-standing, hidden Conservative agenda to weaken the social safety net built over decades. With the Budget, the broken promises and deception of the Conservative Government, it is seen for what it really is-cruel and manipulative. It betrays elderly Canadians. How can the Government ask for

June 17, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
support of Bill C-51 when it betrays in this and in many other ways the trust of Canadian people?
Throughout his budget statement the Minister of Finance continued to use, but in fact abused, the word "confidence". Certainly Canadians are finding it impossible to have any trust in a Minister or in a Government claiming to restore confidence when the Minister's own projections and forecasts for the economy, set out in his Budget Speech, and after taking into account the impact on the economy of that Budget, show a growth rate decline from the 4.7 per cent record increase in 1984, a year of Liberal Government, to 3.1 per cent for 1985 and dropping further to only 2.4 per cent in 1986. Jobs will not be created, unemployment, which is all too high, will not be reduced without a continued and in fact an accelerated pace of economic growth. Because of its own policies as set out in the Budget, the Government admits that it will be causing a slowing of the rate of growth on one hand. On the other hand, it continues to speak of confidence while in fact it puts both hands into the pockets of lower and middle-income Canadians through hidden and sometimes not so hidden tax grabs in its Budget.
This is what we must learn to expect from a Finance Minister who said during his speech to the Canadian Economics Association in Montreal on May 30: "Canada has an acute shortage of rich people". The Minister of Finance does not intend that rich people in Canada should bear their fair share of responsibility. We know this by looking at his Budget. Ordinary Canadians will be taxed an additional $400 to $500 per year when all tax increases in the Conservative Budget are taken into account. There is no stipulation that these revenues will be directed toward the poorer regions of the country, toward unemployed youth, toward elderly Canadians, toward single parents or toward the less advantaged people who need assistance. This money, taken from ordinary Canadians in extra and new taxes, will likely go into the pockets of rich Canadians through new tax breaks like the lifetime capital gains exemption set out in the Budget, as well as through following a blind priority of reducing the deficit rather than a priority of job creation and economic growth.
The Hon. Leader of the Opposition put this point in simple, straightforward terms when he said:
The $500,000 capital gains tax exemption is a cash bonanza of $125,000 ... The average family faces a $500 a year tax, while the wealthy have a cash lifetime bonanza of $ 125,000.
The value of the capital gains exemption has been estimated by the Department of Finance at $1.2 billion in 1990. Only 63 per cent of this capital gains benefit has been shown to go to people earning over $50,000 per year who represent only 4 per cent of Canadian taxpayers. Even if we ignore the effects of the capital gains tax exemption, the family earning only $15,000 annually will pay 36 per cent more in income taxes, while the family earning $200,000 will pay only 2 per cent more.
Is that fair? The answer of ordinary, individual Canadians and their families is that it is not fair. They say that the
Budget and any legislation connected with it should not be allowed to go into effect.
Among the other 96 per cent of taxpayers, most of whom cannot use the capital gains exemption, are old age pensioners. I have already indicated to the House the damage the Conservative Government intended doing to their basic income in the Budget, as presented to the House on May 23. Its program of deindexation, applied not only to the Old Age Security pensions but also to the family allowance and the basic tax payable by individual Canadians, takes desperately needed money from senior and lower and middle-income Canadians and does severe harm to the economy.
If the Government is willing to reconsider the desperate and dangerous mistake it made in intending in its Budget to cut the purchasing power of the pensions of elderly Canadians, why will it not do the same thing when it comes to the purchasing power of middle and lower-income Canadians through the basic family allowance? After all, figures have been presented by reputable bodies such as the Canadian Press and the Canadian Council on Social Development, showing that the net effect of the Conservative Budget of May 23 is to begin cutting family benefits on an income of only $20,000 per year. There are not too many people who will say that such a family income in Canada today is a starting point for wealth; quite the contrary. Budget documents of the Department of Finance, which were not tabled with the Budget because of the truth they contain, show that the Government will take away at least $1.6 billion from pensioners by 1990. It is a well understood fact that pensioners struggling near the poverty line spend this money on the goods and services which they need to live. In addition to the damage to pensioners, the Government is taking $1.6 billion out of the Canadian economy. At the same time as the Government reduces demand in this manner, a leaked Department of Finance document shows that it is piling up a $1.3 billion tax break through its new capital gains tax exemption. This tax break does not even have to be used to invest in productive economic activity in Canada. It is all right, according to the Conservative Government, to invest those gains in condominiums in Florida, in works of art or in jewellery. That is Tory economics; it is not the economics of Canadians generally.
As we predicted before the Budget was brought down, Canadians will be forced to pay an additional nine cents per gallon at the gas pumps after the beginning of September, to pay for tax breaks for multinational oil companies of more than $2 billion by the conclusion of the next fiscal year. Individual Canadians will be hit by an increased federal sales tax and an extension of the sales tax base to candies, soft drinks, pet foods and cosmetics. On top of these and other tax increases required to make up the shortfall of $8.5 billion in revenues from oil industry taxation by 1990, the Government's deindexation measures alone will take $11.5 billion out of the hands of ordinary Canadians and their families in the next five years.
In conclusion, the Budget is built upon shameful principles involving an abdication of fairness and a disregard of fairness.
June 17, 1985

Its economic assumptions are as wrong as the public policy ethics between its lines. It is a mean-spirited scheme which seeks to implement the mistaken belief that deficit reduction above all will provide the conditions for private sector investment and therefore economic growth. On the contrary, it is public policy devoted above all to the goal of economic growth and full employment that in reality creates jobs that provide the tax base needed to reduce government deficits.
The Government has this reality all mixed up. It is undoubtedly, given its own predictions, going to move us backwards when it comes to economic growth. This mean-spirited Budget will cause joblessness and increase poverty and despair among Canadians. This Budget is advanced by a Government that does not, and I think cannot, understand that fairness and justice are integral parts of both the meaning and the generation of economic prosperity. For this reason let us send a message to this mean-spirited Government on behalf of senior citizens, Canadian families, indeed on behalf of all middle and lower-income Canadians, that the Budget is damaging to them and to Canada and thereforre Bill C-51 must be soundly rejected.
