Mr. Speaker, there are a few areas of government policy I would like to comment on in this debate on the borrowing authority which the Government requires to carry on with its platform. First, I would like to comment, as environment critic for my Party, on how the Government is performing with respect to the environment and environmental issues. We notice with some satisfaction that there are no further cuts in the Department of the Environment itself in the Budget as it now stands. I think credit has to be given to many Canadians who let their anger be heard over the cuts in the Canadian Wildlife Service and other areas announced in the statement of November 8. I think the Government, once bitten, is twice shy about cut-backs in the environment. But the real test will come whenever the Nielsen task force reports. If the Department of the Environment and environmental sensitivity survives that report, then indeed Canadians who are concerned about the environment will be able to congratulate themselves on a job well done. They will have made it clear to the Minister and the Government that they did not have a mandate to go ahead with cuts in the Department of the Environment, in the Canadian Wildlife Service, or in the environmental monitoring which was taking place under the National Research Council.
Although Canadians from time to time may not be pleased with things the Government does for which it has a mandate, they are even less pleased when it goes ahead on things it did not seek a mandate for. Surely the Government did not seek a mandate to make cuts in the Department of the Environment. All we have to do now is to get the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) to realize that what she says, where and how she says it, is very, very important, not just for her own political fortunes, however short they may be, but for the well-being of the environment. As I said the other day in the
Borrowing Authority Act
House when she was asking the Canadian Nature Federation to judge her by her actions and not her words, her words are important. If she says, as she did in committee once, that there are people who have worked with PCBs for 30 years and there is nothing wrong with them, well, that is not the kind of argument you expect from the Minister of the Environment. It is reminiscent of the argument made by Rothmans and other cigarette companies 30 years ago-and they might even be making it today-that there are people who have smoked for 40 or 50 years and they do not have lung cancer, so let's not get excited about the causal relationship between cigarette smoking and lung cancer. You cannot have these kinds of gems coming from the Minister of the Environment without there being some anxiety created on the part of those people who are concerned about the environment. If the Minister muses about privatization of the national parks system, this sends out a signal to people who may be interested in exploiting our national parklands for private purposes. The same holds true if she muses about logging and mining in national parks. I am told there are already some logging companies in Alberta who have expressed an interest in that. Since then the Minister has gone some way toward the goal of clarifying her remarks, but she has not ruled out logging and mining in new national parks, and that is still unacceptable to us. In any event, I wanted to put on the record the concern that I and a lot of other people have about the way the Minister is performing.
Members will be aware, I hope, that at this very moment, and since Friday, there has been a blockade going on at Wollaston Lake in northern Saskatchewan having to do with the concern of people there about the extent of uranium mining going on there and its potential expansion. I support that group and I feel for their desperation in trying to get someone to listen. I hope the Minister of the Environment will do the right thing and initiate an environmental review process, which I understand has never really taken place up there, either provincially or federally, regarding the new mines being planned. I hope she will try to initiate a process whereby the people there could be listened to and the effects of these new mines on the renewable resources economy of that area, on the native community and on the environment in general, could be assessed.
To be honest about my own biases in this area, I say that in the context of my opposition to uranium mining anyway. 1 put that opposition on the record when I first came to this place, even when there was a NDP Government in power in Saskatchewan. My opposition has been consistent throughout, and so when I am critical of the provincial Government of the day in Saskatchewan for not doing what I think it should do, 1 want no one to think that I am singling out the Progressive Conservative Government. I think uranium mining is a mistake no matter who is responsible for it and no matter to which Government the Crown corporation involved is responsible. It is one of the most hideous way we have yet developed as a white industrial society of trampling on the lives of native communities. We do this in the name of the international arms

June 17, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
race and sell uranium to countries like France so they can blow up innocent little islands in the Pacific and continue their ecological crimes, sins against the planet which they seem determined to commit regardless of the opinion of the international community, or anyone else for that matter.
I think it is high time that Canada got out of the uranium mining business altogether and said that we do not want to play a part in this. We do not want to be a part of the international uranium system which is part and parcel of the nuclear arms race. We have often got up in this place and been critical about the arms race, yet at the same time we remain silent about that aspect, the uranium mining which is taking place in northern Saskatchewan.
In that context I would call on the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) to institute the kind of public or parliamentary inquiry into the whole nuclear fuel cycle which was promised by the Progressive Conservative Party in 1979. That promise was in its Throne Speech of 1979, but since it came back to power in 1984 we have heard absolutely nothing about such an inquiry. I used to have the impression that that Party was critical of the nuclear future which was imposed on Canada by the Liberals without any real consultation with the public and without any real debate about the role that nuclear power should have in our energy future. I had some hope that that was one area in which the Conservatives might do something I would agree with, but we have had complete silence since the election of September, 1984. When the silence has been broken, there have been statements from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources which are, to put it bluntly, quite frightening. The Minister has said that the only problem with Candu and the whole nuclear power option is a marketing one. That is not a view that goes to the root of the more fundamental question of whether or not this is an energy option that we ought to be pursuing in any event.
With regard to radioactive waste disposal, in a letter the Minister sent to the town of Gimli and other municipalities that passed resolutions expressing opposition to Manitoba becoming a radioactive garbage dump as a result of the research going on at Pinawa, the Minister said that the Government was interested in the commercial aspects of radioactive waste disposal. She went on about how Canada might be able to profit by becoming a repository for the radioactive garbage of the rest of the world. That is what I call a commercial world view taken to its most ridiculous extreme.
1 have taken every opportunity to ask the Government to repudiate its view of radioactive waste disposal, but no word has been forthcoming with respect to whether or not an inquiry will take place. If one were to read the comments made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to the Canadian Nuclear Association the weekend before last, one would get the impression that it is business as usual and that we will see no different action taken by the Conservatives when it comes
to the question of nuclear power except for some of the cuts that we have seen at AECL.
The third thing on which I would like to comment is the underlying values in the Budget. Through this Budget we have learned a lot not just about Tory economics but about Tory values. We have learned more than we ever really wanted to know about those things. The key phrase in the Budget was the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) saying that the Tories wanted to reward success rather than subsidize effort. What does that tell us?
There is a tendency on the part of the Progressive Conservative Members, collectively and individually, to think that the financial world is the real locus of human activity and that everyting else has to play second fiddle to that. That can be seen in the summer job program through which the only jobs that are regarded as worth-while are those which can be hitched to the private sector. Those jobs which may be community oriented and deal with people are put in a kind of second class category because the real jobs are created when a small business hires people to help it market a product that nobody needed in the first place so that it can produce more junk. That is real economic activity as far as Progressive Conservative Members are concerned.
What did we see in the Budget? The Government is going to reward success rather than subsidize effort. What government Members are saying is that it is not how one plays the game of life but it is whether or not one wins. That is the value that lies at the root of the Tory Budget. The Government is telling all those people who do not have $500,000 in capital gains that they are not successful. Government Members do not regard them as the kind of people who make the economy run.
Pensioners on GIS, people who might receive a small company pension, people who worked hard all their lives and raised families but who do not have the level or the kind of incomes that will enable them to benefit from this Budget are not the people who really count. The people who really count are the people who can come into a $500,000 capital gain or be eligible for all the other goodies that are made available to the investment community. As far as I am concerned, that is bribery. It is nothing other than a bribe to rich and powerful Canadians who will not make the effort unless there is a buck in it for them. Pensioners and everyone else will make the effort anyway because they are decent Canadians who would invest their money in this country without even considering buying condominiums in Florida or doing whatever else it is the rich do with their money.
Rich Canadians have to be bribed by their Government to invest in Canada. I say that that is the very kind of economic system that the NDP and before that the CCF were created to resist. That is why we are here. We are here so that we can point the finger at this kind of shallow, immoral economics which makes the ordinary people pay through the nose because they do not have any choice. The rich people for whom there are no borders-their only border is the almighty dollar- might invest their money somewhere else because they do not really care about the country, and so we must cater to them.
June 17, 1985

What Progressive Conservative Members are doing here is capitulating to the very worst elements in our economic system. 1 was never more proud not to be a Progressive Conservative Member than 1 was when I saw 211 Members give their first standing ovation in the Budget Speech to the statement about the $500,000 capital gains exemption. That was one of the grossest things I have seen since I came here. That was the most disgusting display that I have ever seen. Members gave their first standing ovation to the statement about the $500,000 capital gain exemption. Boy, oh, boy, is that not something great for all their constituents?

Mr. Speaker, 1 wanted to comment on the Hon. Member's speech. He began his speech by talking about how the Minister of Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) often shoots from the lip and ultimately backs down on many issues. I think that occasionally the Minister makes really colossal mistakes in the operation of her Department. I believe that she made a colossal mistake last December when she approved the decision made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to cut out the proposed toxicology centre at the University of Guelph. That centre was proposed by two world-famous universities, the University of Guelph and the University of Toronto. It was being supported by the federal Government, the Province of Ontario and the private sector. It was a model about which the Government has been talking-co-operation between the private sector and federal and provincial Governments. It took many years to complete the proposal for the centre. With
Borrowing Authority Act
respect to its funding, the federal Government provided $16 million, the Province of Ontario provided another $16 million, auxiliary assistance was received from the universities, and some $8 million was provided by the private sector. It was a world-class facility which was designed to deal with the toxicological problems of the world. We hear about these problems from newscasts and from concerned Canadians daily, whether it is with respect to the control of diseases and infection in the environment or whether it is leakage problems in the Niagara River. However, the Minister cut that facility which would have given Canada a world-class capacity in dealing with those problems. It would have provided a facility for research and the development of new techniques. It would also have assisted in scientific training. It is a very specialized field. It does not only deal with toxic chemicals, it deals with chemicals which may cause cancer or other diseases which are so prominent in society. I spoke to the Chairman of the Board, who is a research scientist at the University of Toronto, and to other people from the University of Guelph. They indicated that there has been no consultation. The Government thinks that by talking about consultation it makes it so. However, it does not make it so. The decision to cut the centre was a unilateral decision. I am sure even the Hon. Member for Guelph (Mr. Winegard), who is a former President of the University of Guelph, was not consulted. The Minister of Finance simply cancelled the project. There was no consultation with the original team which was appointed to guide the development of the centre.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) was quite right. The Minister often shoots off rockets which she has to retract. However, she also cancels projects such as the centre at the University of Guelph, which will be a severe impediment in the research and training of people in that very important field.
The promise of research and development is simply "Mul-roney baloney". The same applies to the question of indexation, agriculture and the rest of the promises. It is political rhetoric. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has a research audience in front of him, he promises research. When his audience relates to fishery, he makes promises in that area. When his audience is from the agricultural field, he makes promises in that area. The policy of the Government changes every time the audience changes. It is a very serious problem.
Bill C-51 should provide some of the things about which Hon. Members on this side of the House are talking. We are being asked to grant $18 billion of borrowing authority to the Government. The Government made commitments to research, the environment and many other areas. Now the Government is backing off and asking for a blank cheque, with no promises.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the 10 minutes I have available to me, I would like to make some comments on Bill C-51, which is an Act the Government has introduced in order to increase its authority to borrow funds to spend on operating expenses during the course of this fiscal year. As you know, Mr. Speaker, having read the Bill, what the Government is asking for is an additional $18,200 million on top of the borrowing authority which already exists.
Just so that we can compare that borrowing authority with previous ones, I would like to take the House back for a moment to the Minister's speech when he introduced this Bill on May 28. As recorded at page 5133 of Hansard, he said at that time:
With the passage of this Bill, the Government will have a total of $32.2 billion of borrowing authority for the current fiscal year.
Later, on that same page, he compares this year's borrowing authority with the previous year's borrowing authority. He points out that the total amount of borrowing authority for the 1984-85 fiscal year was $31.9 billion. Today we are being asked to increase the borrowing authority by about $300 million over and above what this House allotted the previous administration.
The Government is increasing the amount of money it wishes to borrow after arguing that it was busy cutting deficits, reducing expenditures, and creating an era of confidence in the country. I am wondering what type of signals of confidence are being sent out from a Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) who says he is cutting the borrowing of the country and reducing the deficit, then asks the House for more money than, even to use his assessment of them, the accursed Liberals asked for in the previous year.
Parliament is being asked to give the executive branch of the Government an additional $300 million over and above what it spent in the previous year. Why is this extra money necessary? It does not seem to be for the provision of goods and services. In fact, the Minister of Finance does not seem to have taken any substantive action to reduce the deficit. He has reduced expenditures to a lot of key people. Pensioners will be asked to
take a cut in the real value of their pensions. Families will be asked to take a cut of $500 per year in their spending power based on the May 23 Budget. That falls on top of a tax load imposed in the November 8 statement, which cost ordinary families approximtely $500 in increased taxes and reduced government services.
In the course of less than a year, average families with average incomes will have approximately $1,000 less to spend than they had with previous administrations. Therefore, why does the deficit not seem to be going down? It is not going down very quickly, as even The Globe and Mail has noticed. It points out that the deficit may be trimmed by as much as $1 billion in 1985-86. The forecast would only be for another $1 billion in 1986-87, which would leave the annual deficit at $32.7 billion in a total budget of just over $100 billion. The Minister of Finance is not changing the proportion of deficit very much as compared to previous Ministers of whom he was so critical.
The most important point is how much of the Gross National Product the Minister is going to ask the Canadian people to carry by way of debt charges as compared to previous administrations. One would expect the amount would be going down. However, the Government's own papers indicate that debt charges seem to be growing somewhat faster than the Gross National Product. In fact, by 1990-91 public debt charges will represent about one-half of a percentage point more of the expected Gross National Product than they did in the budget year 1984-85. Even the budget papers indicate an expected increase in the deficit in the next five years. Yet the focus of the rhetoric from that side of the House continues to be on what a great job they are doing of attacking the deficit.
The facts are becoming more clear as Canadians understand what the Budget is about. They can now see that the attack is not on the deficit, but rather on the pocketbooks of ordinary Canadians. The focus of this Budget and of these spending policies is to effect a transfer of income. It seems that the stated policy of the Progressive Conservatives is to have a transfer of investment income from the pockets of those people who have only ordinary amounts of money, or are very poor, to those individuals who are already wealthy in their own right.
I cite a number of budgetary measures to back this up. They are reinforcing a trend that has occurred, even under Liberal Budgets, over the last four or five years. We are now at the point where approximately 4 per cent of the population of the country has control of about 40 to 42 per cent of the country's resources. There has been no effort to redistribute those resources to less fortunate people. In fact, this Budget will exaggerate that process.
To give an illustration of how corporations have been assisted by this process, let us look at income tax paid by individuals and corporations. In 1950, income taxes paid to the federal Government were shared roughly equally between individuals and corporate citizens. By 1980, 70 per cent were paid by individuals and 30 per cent by corporations. Through the Budget provisions of May 23, by 1986-87, 77.3 per cent of income tax will be paid by individuals and a mere 23.6 per
June 17, 1985

cent by the corporate sector. That accretion of wealth by the already wealthy continues.
The move for the virtual elimination of capital gains tax is being sold to the country as a means of allowing the accumulation of capital in hands which will reinvest it. I submit that we have seen programs like this in previous Budgets. The Lalonde Budget contained an ISIP provision which stands for Indexed Securities Investment Program. That afforded people who wanted to invest in stocks the option of setting up an ISIP in order to avoid paying capital gains on most of their profits from stock investments. This Budget almost entirely eliminates the little capital gains tax that was being charged under the Lalonde Budget.
As a result of such government and budgetary policy, shareholders put different requirements on company officials than may be expected by budget makers at the federal level. They do not use the money saved through decreased taxes to start new businesses or hire more people. Instead, they take the safe route and buy up existing small businesses, which often puts people out of work. The actual result is quite opposite to what the budget planners had hoped for. We must recognize that we are not dealing with rational people. They have failed to study what happens in the real economy.
This particular program, as well as the entire Budget, should be opposed. We should all take every opportunity available to explain why we cannot support this Budget.
MO)

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, I assume that means that when we get up and ask questions in the House, Members opposite become very sensitive and notice our presence.
Every day the Government claims to be decreasing the deficit. It is asking Canadians to shoulder the burden of that decrease and is particularly asking senior citizens to shoulder the burden. It is significant to note that when the Government asks for increased borrowing authority we must question everything it says about its intentions to reduce the deficit and the impact its economic policy will have on the economy. Seniors are being asked to disrupt their own economic package to which they have contributed with their hard-earned money over a lifetime. Yet the Government is calling into question its own economic policy and its effectiveness in reducing the
Borrowing Authority Act
deficit by seeking this borrowing authority of SI8 billion. I suggest that it confesses a failure. Deindexing will cut the purchasing capacity of the Old Age Security pension which makes the credibility of the Government's economic policy crucial.
The Government has accused both the Opposition and the media of distorting the reality of these deindexation proposals. However, whether we call it partial deindexing or deindexing the fact is that the purchasing power of seniors will be $100 less next year, $200 less the next and $300 less the year after that, while the cost of the Government's economic policy increases for the senior citizens who have made this country what it is today.
Although the Government claims to be cutting the deficit, its Budget will cut pensions. Furthermore, the fact that the Government is asking for increased borrowing authority shows that its attempts to cut the deficit have been ineffective. At the same time, the impact of this on seniors is very real and will remove real dollars from their pockets.
Perhaps a partial deindexation of pensions could be justified if everyone was sharing in the burden of deficit reduction. However, the Government's Budget is tough and unfair. The Budget is tough on senior citizens and other groups in this country and is particularly unfair because it gives a tax holiday to the very wealthy in this country. Those who will be eligible for this capital gains tax holiday are those with considerable assets. In the meantime, the Government is asking seniors and others to reduce their incomes in order to combat the deficit.
That is why the Budget is unfair and that is also why it is being rejected. More and more petitions are being presented from Members from all sides of the House. Senior citizens and other Canadians throughout Canada are signing petitions and asking the Government to withdraw its deindexation proposals because they recognize that the Budget is unfair and unjust.
Those petitions will continue to come in until the Government has reversed its position on deindexation. The New Democratic Party has a long traditions of supporting pensioners-beginning with the Canadian Commonwealth Federation, which is the Party from which the NDP grew. We are accustomed to calling on Governments to meet the needs of senior citizens. It is important for us to continue that tradition because Governments must realize that we will fight for seniors every time that they are attacked.
In conclusion, the Government's request for increased borrowing authority shows that its efforts to reduce the deficit have not worked. It is understandable that Canadians are outraged when it asks seniors to cut their incomes in the name of deficit reduction. The Government will have to reverse its position on the deindexation of seniors' pensions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have the opportunity to stand before this august assembly to consider Bill C-51, which would accord to

June 17, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
Her Majesty's Government authority for borrowing an additional $18 billion this fiscal year.
I have been listening to the debate. In a certain sense it is rather peculiar. The Government is being berated because it has been observed that it is committed to a redistribution of wealth in favour of the wealthy at the expense of the poor and the elderly. This kind of debate has been deemed by some as rather strange. After all, this is a Conservative Government. What would one expect of a Conservative Government except that it would do what it has set about doing? It should not be of any particular surprise that there should be a capital gains tax exemption in favour of the wealthy. It should not come as a particular surprise that those making over $200,000 per year will pay less taxes, while those making less than $30,000 per year will pay more taxes. It should not come as a particular surprise that more money will be furnished to the oil companies for their benefit at the expense of the rest of us. There are no surprises. This is what one would expect of a Conservative right-wing Government. One must ask why there is so much upset and why there is such a tremendous reaction. Perhaps one could attribute the reaction of so many to the fact that the Government has proved to be so precociously hyprocritical.
I direct the attention of the House to a matter which I think should be of great concern to the Government. It said that it would help out small business persons. I do not know to what small business people Hon. Members of the Party opposite have spoken. However, I know that the small business people to whom I spoke, small retailers, small manufacturers and so on, are a little concerned that $7.6 billion will be taken out of the pockets of consumers next year. They have great difficulty trying to understand why they should be encouraged to invest more, why they should expect to have increased sales, and why increased investment and hiring are justified.
The trouble is that the Government promised to be so different. We had a smooth talking salesman and his colleagues going across the country promising that things would be different. I will always remember the day that the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) seemed almost to declare himself a New Democrat by saying: "I agree with you, Ed; there should be a minimum tax on the rich". However, the promise which hurt was the one given several times, the promise that there would continue to be complete indexation of the Old Age Security. As I said, that promise was thrice given. We have heard about confidence, consultation and sacred trust. It is to be observed that the word "sacred" has come into serious question in the last few weeks.
Many Canadians, including senior citizens and the elderly, were convinced by the smooth performance during the election campaign. They were further reassured in the House, despite the fact that they were somewhat miffed by having a Saturday Night Live show with clackers on the Government side. They had no reason to believe that they would be so treacherously treated as to have experienced a proposal, as it now is, to deindex the Old Age Security.
The problem is that it is very difficult to establish trust, especially for politicians. I am willing to accord to the present
Prime Minister that during the first portion of his tenure he communicated to all of us at least a basis upon which we could trust him, so we thought. So competently, so sincerely and so soothingly presented were his promises that we thought at the very least that he would live up to what he said. He did not. By so doing, he has wrought almost a revolution among senior citizens and elderly of the country. So offensive was the breaking of those promises that no one has been able to produce a single soul representing any significant organization in Canada who is prepared to accept that deindexation of the Old Age Security was a reasonable and just proposal.
I know Hon. Members opposite feel very uncomfortable in the position in which they find themselves. It is a tragedy when the Prime Minister has created an image of hucksterism in that office. It is offensive and dangerous to the democratic process when the slick promises of a vacuum cleaner salesman become the rhetoric of a Prime Minister. It is dangerous when the Prime Minister is imaged as an individual from whom one would not buy a used car. If I were sitting on the side opposite, I would seriously question the future of a Party which has projected an image that has been so viciously contradicted. A Party which has offended the notion of the morality involved in breaking promises in the fashion that has been done is a Party which will be in trouble.
I stood before about 1,200 senior citizens last week and I asked the following question: Is there anyone here willing to stand up and defend the position that senior citizens should sacrifice what little income they have in order to decrease the deficit or to increase the wealth of the wealthy, that they should be the sacrificial lambs for increasing employment? As the record has shown all over the country, not an individual stood up. It is a sad day when the Leader of the country, having projected an image of trust, of assurances to the elderly and the poor, of honesty and of marriage to sacred trust, should so badly translate it into such treatment of those in society who need a more positive thrust in the direction of this country, a thrust to development of employment and economic growth which we should demand and have.
It is not a situation which does any of us proud. I hope we will proceed just a little farther than this backtracking which is already on the record. Canadian senior citizens know that the forces for revision of the Budget are strong even within the Conservative Party. There is no reason to delay. There is no reason to continue the worry, concern and prospect of suffering among senior citizens who will be placed below the level of poverty as a consequence of deindexation. There is no reason the Government should not accede to the demands of virtually every person in the country, live up to its promise and return to an image of trust within its own ideology. I cannot accept that ideology, but at least it should be true to its ideology and to its promises, and then perhaps we could return the debate to a more reasonable basis.

Mr. Speaker, in discussing the borrowing authority, very little
June 17, 1985

attention has yet been paid to the money spent by the Government on international development assistance. Some really quite tragic developments are taking place and are being encouraged by, particularly, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens), apparently without the knowledge or concurrence of either the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) or the Minister for External Relations (Mrs. Vezina). There is a conflict between finance and regional industrial expansion on the one hand, and external affairs and external relations on the other, and it has been growing since the present Government came into power September 4.
You will recall that the Secretary of State for External Affairs announced at the UN that Canada would continue to have a target of .7 per cent of GNP on official development assistance by 1990. Apparently without discussion with that Minister, the Minister of Finance announced in his November statement that the deadline date would be moved from 1990 to 1995. That came as a surprise to everyone since we had taken the Secretary of State for External Affairs' word that the deadline date would be 1990. As I said, that was the beginning.
We then saw the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) get into the act in his January discussion paper on international trade in which he mentioned the desirability of linking trade and aid through something called the trade and development facility. I think he had intended that originally this would be in the Export Development Corporation, where it might indeed very appropriately belong, but it has now suddenly turned up in the Canadian International Development Agency. Indeed, the Minister of Finance in his Budget stated that the trade and development facility would be in CIDA.
Most significant of all, and it seems to me that this has been almost entirely ignored, the Minister also announced that this trade and development facility would receive half of all increases in the foreign aid Budget for the next decade. Apparently this was done again without the knowledge or concurrence of either the Secretary of State for External Affairs or certainly the Minister for External Relations who is responsible for CIDA.
It was some two months later, after the statement of the Minister for International Trade, that the Minister for External Relations decided it was time to consult the non-governmental organizations about this linking of trade and aid. Now the Green Paper comes out with a list of extremely interesting questions which have again been largely ignored because only four paragraphs are devoted to international development assistance. Nevertheless, it is a series of very interesting questions which it would like the public consultation process to help the Government answer.
One of these questions concerns the nature of the linkage between our trade and aid program. This is put as a question in the Green Paper. The Minister has made a great deal of having full consultation with the Canadian public before any decision is taken. Yet, as we have already seen, a decision has been taken that this new facility established in CIDA with its
Borrowing Authority Act
emphasis on trade will receive half of all increases in the foreign aid budget for the next decade. This just shows how little the Government really believes in the consultation process which it talks about all the time.
It was prepared to decide on star wars without consultation. It was prepared to decide on bilateral trade with the U.S. without consultation. It has now agreed to a couple of weeks' consultation this summer and, if you work out the probable agenda for the hearings, as I have been doing, given the translation requirements and notice to all interested groups, it seems to me to be impossible to hold more than two weeks of hearings if the deadline date of August 23 is to be met. That is just a facade, it is not consultation at all.
In the case of trade and aid, the deed has already been done and it has been announced in the Budget. As far as I can see, the Minister for External Relations, who is responsible for CIDA, is watching the Canadian International Development Agency being turned into the Canadian Export Development Agency. The purpose of this new facility in CIDA is to in a sense duplicate the Export Development Corporation, perhaps because it is not doing a good enough job, and provide export subsidies chiefly to uncompetitive and inefficient Canadian businesses.
A second recent development shows that it is not only the Minister of Finance and the Minister for International Trade who are now determining our international development assistance policy, but also the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion.
It is very interesting that while the Minister for External Relations was in San Salvador signing an agreement to provide a loan, presumably for development assistance, to El Salvador despite the continuation of the death squad activities, the special envoy of the Minister for Regional Industrial Expansion, who is a Salvadoran and who at one time I am told worked for the Salvadoran Embassy in Ottawa, was meeting with a small right wing business clique in Salvador, almost all of whose members are participants in the ARENA Party of D'Aubuisson, telling the elite that they would be the conduit for the development assistance being proposed by the Minister for External Relations.
I know the Minister was asked to meet with the Minister for Regional Industrial Expansion for two hours prior to her going to Central America. No doubt she got the word on how the linkage between aid, trade and export subsidies would be facilitated in the loan to El Salvador. What she probably did not know was that the envoy of the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion was in Salvador at the very same time giving guarantees that the aid would be, as is the case in other development which I have mentioned, subsidized trade linked in with the small right wing business community in Salvador.
What this House must do, and in the very near future, is persuade the Government to not continue making the final decisions on linking of aid and trade but to genuinely consult the Canadian public as the Green Paper says it wishes to, and see if the Canadian public would like to see a genuine aid

June 17, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
program or simply one which subsidizes Canadian and other businesses.

On Clause 2-

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Clause 2(2) of the Bill states:
All borrowing authority conferred by subsection (I) that remains unused and in respect of which no action has been taken by the Governor in Council pursuant to Section 37 of the Financial Administration Act shall expire on March 31, 1986.
Would the Minister of State for Finance, in requesting such a large amount, enlighten us on the projections of the President of the Treasury Board? His November statement dealt with the raising of additional revenues to the Government of
June 17, 1985

Canada by increasing fees and eliminating certain programs. Could the Minister indicate to the House whether or not the projections by the President of the Treasury Board and the Minister of Finance are on line, in view of the fact that many Ministers have cancelled fund raising activities; funds which were supposed to be derived from increasing certain fees. What effect would those modifications in the financial statements have on the requirements of the Government of Canada and the requirements as stated in the borrowing authority Bill?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the changes that have been instituted since the original projections in the fall, based on the kind of fees that the Member is talking about, would be marginal at best.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I imagine that they are marginal in the Minister's eyes when we are talking about $18.2 billion. However, even the smallest projection made in each Government Department means something to that Government Department.
Would the Minister reconsider her answer? Projections have been made by each Minister as to how much the Government of Canada would gain from increased fees as a result of modifying certain fee schedules and modifying the collection of fees from the general public in many areas. Many of these announcements have since been cancelled. In other words, there were subtantial modifications made by every Minister since the November financial statement and since the Ministers made statements regarding the increased revenues to the Department.
If the Minister finds it difficult to understand what I am talking about, let me give her an example. The Department of the Environment said it would raise fees by charging people for telephone calls. As I understand it, that will not now be done. It also said it would save the Government of Canada money by cancelling park guides. That will not be the case. There are a number of examples of increased fees for public usage which have since been cancelled.
Surely the Minister cannot say that these millions of dollars are only marginal. Surely the Minister must have some opinion as to what the effect of those cancellations have been as a result of public uproar in various parts of the country? What effect will that have on the needs of the Government of Canada under this borrowing authority?
Does it give further reason for the inclusion of Clause 2(2) as outlined in the Bill?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:

Member will check the Main Estimates again, he will discover that the rate of increase in Government spending is at its lowest in many years. subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:

The Minister is supposed to be an expert on this Bill and is supposed to give the House some general opinion of the requirements of the Government of Canada as outlined under this borrowing authority. All that she has told the House so far is that the effects will be marginal because it is only a few hundred million dollars, give or take a few hundred million.
1 am asking the question in all sincerity. Has the Government re-examined its financial needs for this financial year in view of the modifications and changes that have been made since the President of the Treasury Board outlined the vicious cuts in Government Departments and projected increases in revenues amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars? Much of that is from programs that have been reinstituted or changed from the collection of higher fees to the collection of lower fees. Surely the Minister knows what 1 am talking about. subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: That means she doesn't know.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if the changes are marginal and do not really have any effect on the needs of the Government of Canada, why is there this increase in fees in the November statement? If it is only marginal, why is so much attention being paid to it by Ministers of the Crown? Surely it is not only marginal. Surely the President of the Treasury Board could stand in his place and tell us what the negative figure has been since his November statement?
Members of the House deserve to have this information. You cannot have a Government operating like this, saying that it needs $18.2 billion, give or take a billion dollars, and just letting it go at that. It is then said in Clause 2 that anything left over will terminate March 31, next year.
Surely we deserve some information regarding the actual figures. What happened since the President of the Treasury Board tabled his statements of cuts and increased revenue measures to the Government of Canada? Surely with such a blanket proposal, the House deserves some statement from the Government regarding its needs for the coming year? If it is not forthcoming, maybe I should give an hour long speech on some of these cuts and decreases in revenue. Maybe that would be a good idea. I am calling upon the Minister to take a stab at answering the question which has been directed to her or, as I said, I can go into specifics regarding the difficulty with which the Government of Canada will be faced as far as realizing certain objectives are concerned.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the Hon. Member will find our projections in the Budget. There are some on page 12 and some on page 13. They are public documents. They have been tabled in the House. If he is having difficulty with this, I suggest that he look it up.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have a few comments to make about the particular Clause; perhaps some Hon. Members would like to have a cup of coffee. It is not a joke or a laughing matter. When we examine the document entitled Expenditure and Program Review, tabled in November 1984 by the President of the Treasury Board, it is no laughing matter that we see in every government Department tens of millions of dollars being required and being obtained by the Government of Canada through increased fees to the general public. It is not a laughing matter when the Government of Canada tells everyone that they have to pay for their telephone calls to the weather office. The Government of Canada should be encouraging fishermen and everyone else who needs weather updates to telephone the weather office, not discouraging them. It is no laughing matter to have the Minister of the Environment increasing park fees to such a degree.

I hear the Hon. Member. 1 would like to tell her that they just came out a couple of days ago in our region. They were some of the hidden costs. There will be approximately $9.2 million in increased revenues for the Department of the Environment through increased user fees in national parks.
What does that mean? I will tell the committee what it means for a family. It means in Terra Nova National Park in Newfoundland that to tie up or moor one's boat, the charge will start at $110 for the season and go up to $590. In view of the imposition of that kind of fee scheduling in national parks, I say to the Minister of State for Finance that people will not use the mooring facilities or the wharfs. Therefore that $9.2 million will be substantially reduced.
Let me look at another fee in national parks, the one related to the use of golf courses. It will cost a family over $500 per season. Obviously people will not use the golf courses on a regular basis. Therefore the $9.2 million will be reduced even further.
In that same "little" saving, according to the Minister of State for Finance, we also see an increase in the cost of semi-serviced lots for people using camp facilities. To what will the increase amount? According to the Government of Canada, it must be equal to or more than that offered by private enterprise. Consequently those charges have risen to exceed those of private enterprises adjacent to national parks.

speechtext: Equal to.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I hear the hon. gentleman across the way. 1 should like to tell him something. The fee for a semi-serviced lot in the Terra Nova National Park is over $8. Since the Hon.
Member wants me to get specific, in Beothick Park at East-port, the charge is $7.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: I didn't say that.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Perhaps he did not say it, but I will tell him in any event. Even down at Trinity Cabins, the charge is $7. The Government's increase is a substantial one over the rates charged by private enterprise. There is no place in Newfoundland where one has to pay to moor a boat, so what did the Department say? It said that it would have to go by a national standard of dockage fees somewhere in central Canada. At what did the Department look when it looked at golf course fees? It said that it could not compete with private enterprise, so it would increase the rates more than those of private enterprise.
Apart from that, things have happened to the Government since these projections were made which could substantially impact upon its requirements. I give as an example for the Minister of State for Finance the protectionist tariffs imposed by the Government of the United States on Crown corporations involved in international marketing practices. Obviously they will impact upon the requirements of Crown corporations which, by law, would have to be written off by the Government of Canada. The Government cannot say that they will not have any impact at all.
The Prime Minister is in his own riding tonight attending a meeting. He has to answer to 700 fish plant workers who are being discriminated against by the United States protectionist tariff on saltfish. These workers went to the Prime Minister prior to the Quebec Summit and told him that this problem would arise. The Prime Minister indicated that he would raise it with the President of the United States and that he thought there would not be any problem. On Thursday night, at nine o'clock, down comes the decree from the United States Department of Commerce indicating that there would be a 20.75 per cent tariff on saltfish from the north shore of Quebec, affecting the riding of the Prime Minister, my riding and several other ridings represented in the House. That does not have to be made up by private enterprise. That has to be made up by an agency of the Government of Canada, and that one action will cost that agency millions and millions of dollars. It has been established by law that that Crown corporation must buy all saltfish from fishermen in its coverage area, which includes the entire Quebec north shore and all of Newfoundland.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: And Labrador.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
And all of Labrador, yes. I am not talking about the tariff imposed on saltfish as it relates to private companies. They have been subjected to an 11 per cent or 12 per cent charge by the Government of the United States, but in this case with 20.75 cents on the dollar, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans will have to come up with the difference to make up for the tariff.
The Minister of State for Finance should realize that when establishments which are in place as a result of regulations.
June 17, 1985

Crown corporations, announce to fishermen in the riding of the Prime Minister, or for that matter in any riding in Newfoundland or Labrador, a new price structure for the coming year, as was done three weeks ago, they have to pay that money. On top of that, fishermen have to be compensated for the U.S. tariff. They cannot compensate by charging fishermen less because by law this particular corporation announced its fee structure.
I have another example for the Minister of State for Finance. The Government indicates that it will triple the rates. After looking at the statement of the Hon. President of the Treasury Board, who was only doing what he was ordered to do by Cabinet in November 1984 and in the subsequent statements emanating therefrom, we see that the cancellation of several federal government programs was announced. For example, the cancellation of the fisheries vessel insurance program was announced. What did the Liberal Opposition do in this Chamber? It rose and said that the Government could not cancel it, that it had to reverse its decision. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans rose and said that that program could be cancelled because the President of the Treasury Board said so. However, as time went on, and as we in the Opposition put on the pressure, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans realized that he could not cancel that program and that therefore he could not save the projected $8 million. He could not save the money, so what did he do? He turned around and said that he would triple the rates. We are back into the same situation of having tripled rates and fishermen, who do not require it because the loan authority does not demand it, are not getting the insurance. In that event the projection of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans as far as the $8 million is concerned goes completely out the window.
The Minister of State for Finance and the President of the Treasury Board have to go back to the drawing board. They should ask the Minister of Labour what he is going to do when every provincial administration says that he has to increase the federal minimum wage. What will that do? It will increase the cost of every single contract the Government has with security companies and cleaning companies in airports. It will increase charges to the Government through the Department of Public Works and the Department of Supply and Services.
The Government has to increase the minimum wage. It said it was not going to do it, but I say it will have to do it and very quickly because the federal minimum wage, for the first time in our history, is less than that of any province in Canada. Tory times are hard times. In your province, Mr. Chairman, the minimum wage is $4.58 an hour and the federal minimum wage is $3.50 an hour. That cannot continue because it violates the Labour Code. The Code does not spell it out directly, but it does say that it must reflect the average minimum wage rate across Canada and there is no way the Government can get out of it. But it has not included that in any financial statement or expenditure review program.

There are big gaps in the program announced by the Government to raise fees, increase rents and everything else. You know that a lot of these programs have been cancelled or reorganized. So the question to the Minister was a perfectly logical question and 1 would be pleased now to take my seat and-

Member well knows, they will have to be approved by the House, will they not?

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, 1 do not think the Minister completely understands what 1 am talking about.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: George, I can hardly wait.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Right now, at this very minute, the Government of Canada has decided to cut back on person years in its various departments.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: What?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: To cut back on person years. We used to call it man years, now it is person years.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: The Minister understands that.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The Government notified every federal Department that there must be a cut-back in the number of people hired in the Departments. The Government talks about savings in person years, but nowhere in the financial statements or the Budget papers does it indicate what the increased costs will be to the Government. Yesterday we heard the Government was going to cut back the number of RCMP officer in certain

June 17, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
airports. They will be replaced by private security companies. It is one thing to do that, but it is another thing when Government Departments bring in an employee who has been working for 19 years, as was the case with one I had the other day, or 10, 12, or 13 years, and saying to them that we cannot afford to pay them because our person-years have been cut. However, we will offer you a personal contract. 1 do not see that in the Department of Supply and Services' envelope, Mr. Chairman.
For example, what actually happens is that 350 employees of the Small Craft Harbours section of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans across the country will be offered a personal contract or be hired through a private engineering or consulting company to do their work. As a result, all those Departments which have been cut back will now have to supply money to the Department of Supply and Services to pay for those personal contracts, or that Department will have to pay.
Here is the shame of it. With that policy, the Government still has to pay wages, overtime and an amount to make up for the loss of benefits, but it also has to pay a profit to the person who is hiring the worker concerned. So when you ask the Department of Supply and Services how much extra that person-year is going to cost the Government, they say from 25 per cent to 30 per cent more. But what do you see when you look at the financial papers? You see a saving because of cuts in person-years. There are orders given to Government Departments to cut back on this or that function or to cancel this or that program. There are only six or seven small craft harbours people who are in the field now in Newfoundland. There are only 10 or 12 of them in Nova Scotia and 30 or 40 in Quebec. However, this adds up to about 300 people. This measure in the budgetary papers appears on only one line.
However, these people are losing their positions as public servants. They are losing their pensions and all of their benefits for all time and they are being offered a personal contract or the opportunity to work through a private consulting firm. These people are professional engineers. They have always done that type of work. They go to the communities along the coastline of eastern Canada and the Arctic to help build wharves, slipways or breakwaters. They consult with local community groups who apply for what we used to call Canada Works programs before the present Government got its hands on them. We do not know what that program will be called in the fall.
It is true that the service to the community groups and the local organizations will still exist. However, it will exist at an increased cost to the Government of Canada. It is not, as the budgetary papers would show, a reduction in the cost of Government. It is not a reduction in the amount of money required just because there is a reduction in person-years. It is actually an increase to the expenditures of the Government of Canada because it has to pay for those contracts, either directly or indirectly.
Let me deal with another area that is hazy. I am again discussing the Minister of Labour and a matter that has not even been discussed in this Chamber. It is a matter that should have been discussed; there are a great many matters like that.
The announced reductions in the Expenditure and Review Program of the President of the Treasury Board and the statement made by the Minister of Labour indicate that the Government is going to save money by cutting 25 per cent of the budget on the home repair program across Canada. That shows up as a 25 per cent reduction in the Expenditure and Review Program and in the Budget papers. This works both ways. In this particular case, the reduction will be greater than 25 per cent. Why is that?
1 do not think that the cuts contained in these Budget papers and the Expenditure and Review Program was completely fair. Newfoundland got cut by 44 per cent and Quebec got cut by 48 per cent while the national average was 25 per cent. How the Government arrived at those figures, I do not know. However, when this cut was made, the Department, the Minister, the President of the Treasury Board, the Minister of Finance and all Members of this Chamber did not realize something.
When the cuts went into place only a month ago, all of these offices that administered the program that was cut by 25 per cent through this Expenditure and Review Program could no longer exist. They existed on the fees that they received for the number of applications they processed. That figure was an average of $450 across the country, $500 if it was a municipality and $1,300 if it was in the north. The salaries of the clerks, inspectors and managers were paid on the basis of the number of applications that were processed. Along comes this Expenditure and Review Program which cuts everything across the nation by 25 per cent and cuts some provinces by more than 40 per cent. All of a sudden these offices were left with one-third of the money they had to spend last year, money on which they were just getting by. They could not process enough applications to maintain their existence. The offices are therefore closing down.
The Minister of Labour should know about this. Obviously his advisors have told him that last year some areas were extended for coverage under this home repair program. Big announcements were made in every single province of Canada indicating that the Government would extend this program, just like it did last spring. All of a sudden the Government was left with all of these extended areas but a budget that was cut by 25 per cent. All organizations that were operating the RRAP program got hit twice. They got hit by the reduction of 25 per cent and they got hit with another reduction because the areas of coverage were extended.
What are we now left with? We are left with hundreds and hundreds of homeowners in every single community in this country who are being told that they are too far down on the list to be serviced. However, they were told last year that their turn was coming up next. Now the CMHC and the provincial housing authorities are devising criteria so that they can knock people off the list. If they have a list containing 500 families

June 17, 1985
and they know that they cannot deliver, they say that they are going to restrict the criteria and make it more difficult to qualify.
This is happening when all of these people felt that the home repair program was a cheap way to get their homes repaired, because anyone could get a loan to cover the cost. If one was a millionaire, one could still get a loan. Anyone qualified for a loan. The public felt that this was a great program. All homeowners needed to do was establish the fact that they needed that loan, based on the size or condition of their dwellings and the size of their families. Now, because of this new measure brought about by the reduction in expenditures, there are hundreds upon hundreds of people who will not be able to receive the benefits of the program which has been hit by the 25 per cent cut.
The Minister of Labour cannot now turn around and tell the Minister of State for Finance that he needs additional money because the program was not only cut by 25 per cent but was knocked out of half the country. Now all these areas of Newfoundland no longer qualify because there are no longer any RRAP offices in operation. The provincial administrations refused to operate the program and, since they refused to operate the program and pay the salaries, those offices have to close.
The Minister of State for Finance should realize a couple of realities as they relate to eastern Canada. There has been one of the worst fishing seasons in living memory. The ice is still blocked in on certain parts of the coastline. Fishermen are unable to fish. Fish plants are unable to operate. Even in areas where the ice went out, the water is still too cold for fish. If the water is very cold, the fishermen cannot fish.
Now the Government of Canada has made an about turn. The Minister of Justice announced on behalf of the Minister of Employment and Immigration that the Government would extend unemployment insurance benefits for fishermen this year because the fishery is bad. What was the mistake which was made in the submission to Cabinet, that was approved, which appears in the expenditure program of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans?
The error was that the Government thought that it was just as bad a year this year as it was two years ago when a similar program was implemented. In other words, the Government is going to be faced with the reality this week of having to approve more money for that program. Once the Government has announced it, it cannot stop it. The Government cannot tell people that they will receive an extension of unemployment insurance benefits and then say that it only meant to provide an extension of two weeks. The announcement indicated that the benefits would be extended until the ice was gone and the fishermen could once again fish. That is what was in the announcement of the Minister. Therefore, the Government of Canada, because of the adverse weather conditions, the temperature of the water, and the ice that surrounds the coastline, knows that it must cough up more money in order to satisfy

that program and the terms and conditions which were announced by the Minister of Justice.
Changes will have to be made before the end of the summer. The Minister of Employment and Immigration recognizes that some changes will have to be made as far as her general policy is concerned. She said that she would save $250 million. The Minister of State for Finance probably is thinking that $250 million is only marginal. However, $250 million would reduce the borrowing authority to only $18 billion! Presently it is only $18.2 billion! The Minister of Employment and Immigration has announced that she will not need approximately $200 million this year because of reductions and redefinitions within the Department that controls unemployment insurance. The figure that is used in the Expenditure Review Program is absolutely crazy.
The Minister cannot say in a financial review that she will save $200 million in the coming year because modifications will be made to the interview process for unemployment insurance purposes. I would like to tell the House why that is wrong. The Minister is talking about bringing people into an unemployment insurance office and interviewing them. The Minister is talking about picking up the telephone in every office and asking people if they are looking for work. If those people cannot be reached-Mr. Chairman, I see that my time has expired.
I am sorry that there is not another Clause in the Bill. I have not yet said what I wanted to. However, I suppose my time has expired. I will conclude by saying that in passing this Bill we will give the authority to the Government of Canada to borrow $18,200,000,000, give or take $600 million!

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have a number of questions I want to ask the Minister of State for Finance. I know that the House would like to pass this Bill quickly, but I would remind the Minister that the Bill involves $18 billion. subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would be very happy to tell the Hon. Member what is the current amount of the deferred corporate tax. However, I would first like to explain to him that the most important expenditure which the Government makes is on the interest on the debt. The interest on the debt is $22.6 billion. That is more than we are able to pay for health care, Old Age Security and other things. It is because of that debt that we must borrow this money. Had we not inherited the profligate record of the former Government, we would not be in this position and we would be able to get on with the job of managing the Government and the programs in which we, as a Government, are so interested.
The good management which we have brought to the Government is a record in which we take some pride. Our expenditures show the lowest increase in 17 years. Ministers are managing their Departments in a manner which keeps their

June 17, 1985

expenditures under close control. We have been able to establish an exceptionally good record for expenditures on training and employment initiatives which involve the private sector and local communities as well as the federal Government. It is very important for the Hon. Member to know those things. He should also recognize the efforts which we have made in inflation control and in bringing the debt to a level we will be able to manage much more effectively in future years.
I should also point out to him that in response to the wishes of the House, and as an act of good management, the Borrowing Authority Bill was introduced within two days after the presentation of the Budget. Of course, that means that our figures are up to date. We recognize the connection between having good records before the House and being able to make an assessment of the amount of borrowing authority which will be required. The responsible actions which we have taken are a very important part of the future financial management practices of the Government. The fees to which the former Member referred are part of our management practices. I believe that we have established the most appropriate way to deal with the deficit and the accumulated debt. As a result, we will be able to ask for less borrowing authority next year than would otherwise be required.
One of the important items we have brought forward-and I know the Hon. Member will be interested in it-is the review of corporate taxation. That review will be under way shortly. We are looking at all the measures we use in the corporate sector to raise money. We are also looking at how the corporate tax structure should be changed so that it will be fair and equitable, and will raise the revenues the Government needs. That will give us more flexibility in revenue and expenditure planning.
We are attempting to ensure that Canadian people have the jobs and the social policy framework which they require for the future. And I think what we have attempted to do in the small sector is going to be very important to that.
In response to the direct question, I will get back to the Hon. Member with the answer. I might tell him, however, that the underlying principle of classification, of course, as between budgetary and non-budgetary transactions, is that transactions changing the net indebtedness of the Government are classified as budgetary while transactions involving the creation of an offsetting financial asset or liability are non-budgetary. For example, a loan by the Government increases financial assets since the recipient incurs an obligation to repay the loan. And the creation of the asset for the Government is offset either by a reduction in another asset, which is typically cash, or a corresponding increase in a financial liability, which is typically unmatured debt. I am sure that answers the Hon. Member's question.

Mr. Chairman, when the Minister of State for Finance and her colleagues promised the sky to voters last summer, did they not realize that they might have to face the music some day and pay for those promises? Can she and her front-bench colleagues not add and subtract? There is no justification for getting up in the House day after day and saying that they cannot do it because of the debt situation in the country. There was a debt situation last summer which they talked about all the time, but they still went ahead and made all kinds of promises. The Prime Minister even went to the extent of putting his name on a telex sent to the Chalk River Nuclear Laboratories in my riding of Renfrew-Nipiss-ing-Pembroke. He said not to worry one bit, that not only were they going to retain the present research facilities, they were even considering expanding them. Did the Prime Minister not realize at the time that there had been deficit budgeting in the country? Did he make that promise seriously? Obviously not.
The Government has just chopped 50 per cent from research and development in Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. The Chalk River Nuclear Labs are a very important part of that research and development. For the Prime Minister to go back on a promise is unforgivable, just as it is unforgivable for people on the front benches of the Government to state day in and day out that they did not know the country was in debt so they cannot keep their promises. Is that what the Prime Minister meant when he told the senior citizens of this country that their financial situation was a sacred trust?
The Minister of Finance introduces a Budget, along with the Minister of State for Finance and the Cabinet, that knocks out the first 3 per cent of indexing of the inflationary increase from the pensions of senior citizens of this country. The Government thought it could get away with this by saying that it would provide jobs for the children and grandchildren of pensioners. However, senior citizens of this country are smarter than the front bench of the Conservative Government because they can see through that ploy very easily. The Government is simply trying to make itself look good by cutting back.
A review of history shows that when Marc Lalonde left the finance portfolio, there was a $30 billion debt. When the Conservative Government took office, it ran that debt up to $38 billion and brought it back to $34 billion, then suggested that it had made great progress. That is their logic.
Since the Conservatives follow their great process of consultation, did the five or six conservative MPs from the Ottawa area suggest to the Minister of State for Finance that the

Public Service of Canada should be cut by 15,000? Did they support that concept? Was it the Minister of National Health and Welfare who suggested to the Government that it cut research and development in Atomic Energy of Canada Limited by $100 million? He has Whiteshell in his constituency, another AECL facility. I doubt very much that he made that suggestion.
The Prime Minister of the country not only promised but made a commitment to the Chalk River Nuclear Laboratories that there would be no cuts in that institution. He knew full well at the time that there had been deficit financing in this country. The Government cannot deny that there was insincerity in that promise and that it was absolutely unfulfilled. Not only did he not fulfil that promise, the Government wants to make itself look good by removing money that those labs have managed to earn. It will lift $50 million from AECL's reserves this year and another $20 million from its reserves next year and are applying it to the national debt. Those labs will be left with nothing to back up the situation they will be facing as a result of the $100 million cut on research and development.
One of the platforms on which the Government ran during the election was that it would increase research and development in the country and fully encourage it. The Minister of State for Science and Technology, who has four degrees behind him, went to the Chalk River Nuclear Laboratories to visit the scientists and declare his friendship. He is certainly not a friend today. He is following the Government without any sympathy for the fact that $100 million is being but back from research and development, which is 50 per cent of the Government grant to that institution.
We are sometimes told not to raise the question of the Avro Arrow because there is no comparison. I say that there is a comparison because Atomic Energy of Canada Limited has some of the finest engineers, chemists, physicists, and scientists in the country. Furthermore, the Government is driving the talent away from the National Research Council. It cannot stand success.
It took years to build a success story in research and development in this country. For example, cheap hydroelectric power has been produced through the nuclear reactors in this country. The Province of Ontario alone has saved the residents of Ontario billions of dollars in energy costs by providing energy from Candu reactors. Canadians take it for granted that everyone knows about these successes, but obviously the Government does not know. Without those reactors which produce the cheapest form of hydro that can be found, central Ontario, the home of the Minister of State for Finance and the Minister of Finance, would not have the energy resources to run those industries, factories and businesses in Toronto.
The Minister of Finance talks about rewarding success. However, the way he rewarded success was to chop 50 per cent from the research budget of the very people in AECL who have saved Canadians billions of dollars in energy costs alone. The Government cut $100 million from the research and development budget of AECL and also took $70 million from its reserves without warning. Furthermore, it has proposed no

Again, the Government is downgrading one of the finest research establishments in the country. I was told by one Member that it is not paying its way. However, that is another story. Many companies, both domestic and foreign international companies are related to the nuclear industry in this nation. They send programs to the Chalk River Nuclear Laboratories and other facilities at AECL to conduct research and development. It is saying: "Okay, tomorrow you face the music; we will not give you any more money for it or any time to bridge the gap."
