Mr. Chairman, the concerns we feel about creation of employment in order to get this country back to 4 per cent unemployment do not need any lectures from the Minister.
To return to the topic I was raising a moment ago and picking up on what my friend from Kamloops-Shuswap had to say dealing with deferred taxes and corporate tax expenditures, let the record show that a good hour of questioning of the Minister has not given us the total of deferred corporate taxes. I do not doubt that the search through the records and the guesstimation required would produce an astonishing figure. Surely tens of billions of dollars have gone uncollected, have had to be borrowed and added to the national debt because of this situation. The key point is there has not been any change in nine months of this Government. Nor was there much change in the nine months of the previous Conservative Government.
The question I have for the Minister, one which interests every taxpayer in this country, is what the grand total might be of taxes not collected but which have been turned into capital for Canadian companies or distributed to shareholders. If the total were to reach $100 billion, something over half of the national debt, that is money on which interest is being paid by taxpayers now for the enrichment of corporations and wealthy Canadians. This Government and these Ministers, present and absent, do not intend to do a damn thing about it by the appearance of things. There has been little talk about looking at corporate taxes, but it is primarily at where the losses could be pulled in so as to reduce one's tax burden.
The taxpayers of this country have been told this year they are going to pay three times as much tax as the corporations do, about 45 cents out of every dollar Ottawa takes in comes from individuals and only 15 cents from corporations. Taxpayers have been flimflammed by this Government talking about the enormous national debt, but they want to know exactly how much of the wealth of Canada was taken out of their pockets. They want to know exactly what proportion of their taxes is the result of allowing nine corporate family groups to acquire something like half of the stock traded in the TSE 300. They want to know exactly how much this Government and previous Liberal Governments have taken from their pockets in the process of making a handful of Canadians spectacularly wealthy.
It is appalling that a Government which has been in office for nine or ten months does not have any idea of what those figures are. It is surely appalling that a Government which would pride itself on being business-like has no idea what those figures are. Individual taxpayers of Canada, those people we have talked about ad nauseam, as the Government would probably say, have a very great interest in knowing exactly how much of their tax burden is the result of this transfer of wealth. They want to know if these cut-backs by the Government are the result of taxes not collected from the wealthy.
If ordinary Canadians saw that figure, they would be astonished. It is quite possible that $100 billion is an underestimate. The borrowings being undertaken by the Government now
Borrowing Authority Act
move us up toward a debt of $200 billion. If ordinary Canadian taxpayers were to realize that this supposedly business-like Government is in fact a Government from Wall Street and Bay Street and does not give a damn about them and is quite ready to let this game go on, there would be a revolt in this country which would make the pensioners protest over the last few weeks look like just the beginning.
I suggest to the Minister of State for Finance and her colleague the Minister of Finance that it is time we knew what a reasonable estimate of corporate tax expenditures will be. It is time we knew what the deferred taxes totalled. We have a right to know exactly how much of the national debt is money that ordinary Canadians are paying to enrich corporations and their owners, and in particular a small number of the wealthiest Canadians. That is the kind of capitalism that exist in this country today.
I really do not believe it is true for all of them, but if Conservative Members really want to continue with that kind of refined exploitation of our tax system both on the corporate break side and the individual burden side, let them be clear with the public that that is what they want to do. They will discover the extent to which the voters of 1988 or 1989 will reject this Government.
With those comments, I would invite the Minister to give us any kind of firm figure she might have on corporate tax breaks. Is she able to tell me that the total which I have suggested is outrageously high, and that individual Canadians are not paying anything like that total to enrich a few, or is she not? Does she have to confess the ignorance of the Finance Department and the imperative need to get on with the job of gathering information in order to make the national accounts of this country as business-like as they ought to be?

Mr. Chairman, the Minister did not answer my question; not that I really expected she would have the resources at hand to do so. She began responding to the speech which dealt with the Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, undoubtedly a good topic to consider as well.
The Bill indicates that a sum of money may be required for public works and general purposes. The public works part is the part that interests me. In recession circumstances, when some industries are concerned about the possibility that they may be sliding into depression circumstances, public works are one of the means available to us for maintaining and increasing employment and for increasing economic activity.
As I suggested earlier today, the budget speeches of the early 1930s, the Bennett days, provide some interesting reading. I concede that much has changed over the years and Ministers of Finance are less involved with the details of their accounts than they were in those days. I suppose that is the point I have been making over the past 15 minutes. There was a good deal less moralizing going on in speeches made in those days than is the case these days.
One of the interesting things about the budgets of the 1930s is that when the R. B. Bennett Government first came in, Mr. Bennett recognized the need for a jolt of expenditure so that the Government would not simply be paying out relief costs. Therefore, some public works authorizations were put forward. There had of course been others which the Liberal Government in earlier years had put forward as well.
I think we have a similar situation today. We had a Conservative Government in office which, very early, has denounced the waste and extravagance of its predecessor. It took a little longer to do so in the 1930s. However, in various areas, I find that the concern of my constituents and people

I can tell that is true. For those who were not listening, the Minister has just said that she has been looking forward to this all day.
I was not going to rise and speak in this debate, as I thought that things were going along reasonably well. However, I heard the Minister say that somehow or other she took some joy from the fact that there are 271,000 people working who otherwise might not have been working. I cannot help but feel a sense of panic in my heart when I hear such a statement. There are still approximately 1.8 million people who are unemployed. For a Minister of the Crown to rise an expect that we should applaud when the Government has created a paltry 271,000 jobs, over and against the enormous need, is enough to make one shudder.
The Minister has failed to address the areas of greatest need, those in the age group of 16 to 24 and those in the age group of 55 to 65. There continues to be an overwhelming number of people who are almost to the point of being institutionally unemployed. That is not being addressed by the Government.
The Government has asked us to allow it to borrow additional funds. To do what? We are not clear on that. The Government says it needs more money. I know the minister will remember the discussion on the Government's proposal to partially deindex old age pensions. We suggested to the Government places where it could go to raise substantial amounts of dollars-into the billions of dollars-in order to offset a number of tax impositions which the Government was prepared to impose. The Government said no. My colleague from Kamloops-Shuswap suggested one area. I see that my colleague from Simcoe North is in the Chamber. As a lawyer and an accountant, he has gone through the analysis quickly and can see the point which we have made.

How can the Government ask the House of Commons to permit it to borrow money to pay for the debt it has accumulated on behalf of extremely wealthy corporations which are not paying taxes? That does not seem to be an unreasonable point to make. Is it not reasonable to expect that the corporate sector, in these difficult times, would perhaps be willing to contribute, if not the amount it owes, at least the interest costs to the balance of society on the money it owes? The Minister is shaking her head. I am not sure whether it is because she has never thought of that before or, perhaps, it is the first time that she has considered it. Who else in society, other than corporations, can come to the Government and ask the Government to borrow money in order to pay what they rightfully owe and then not even pay a cent toward interest charges? It does not take much to see the unfairness of that.
There are a lot of people in the country who have not worked for the past year. They are drawing on savings which they have accumulated over 30 or 40 years. Those people are receiving a bill from the Department of National Revenue which tells them that they owe the Government some tax. If those people asked the Government to defer the tax for a few years, and if they also asked not to pay interest charges, can we imagine the Government's response? This Government and its predecessor, which I might say are cut from much the same cloth-the two political Parties which represent a vested interest in Canada-allow those who have more than they need to not pay taxes. If they should happen to be asked to pay a share, by God, the Government will give them all kinds of loopholes so that they will not have to pay their share. It is not only the corporate sector which gets away with that. Heaven forbid that we should only allow deferred taxes without any payment-

Mr. Chairman, I am being asked if I will change the Ontario Corporation Tax Act. That shows the naivety of the Member. He knows that I have no power to change the Ontario Corporation Tax Act.
That provision is not only provided to the corporate sector. I might add that the corporate sector owes many billions of dollars.
I want Tory back-benchers to tell me the truth. How many of them truly believe that it is fair to tax a widow on her pension and to say to the corporate sector that it can defer taxes and that the Government will borrow money in the international money markets to cover what the corporate sector would normally have to pay? The Government does not even ask the corporate sector to pay interest on that money. Do they think that is fair? Is there one Tory who is prepared to stand and say that he thinks a widow should have to pay tax in order to cover the costs which ought to be borne by the corporations, upon whose behalf we borrow money so that they
Borrowing Authority Act
will not have to pay taxes? I do not see Members rising, so I assume that they all agree with me.
It is not only the corporate sector, it is those who benefit from the corporate sector. What has the Government done with those guys? The Government says: "Well, you are not getting enough out of that so we will allow you to accumulate half a million dollars in your lifetime tax-free. However, we cannot do that for everybody. If we are going to do that it can only be for the top 5 per cent of the population." That will cause problems for the Government.
Not only will the Government allow corporations to defer taxes and to not pay interest charges, it will now give an additional bonus to those individuals in the top 5 per cent so that they can accumulate $500,000 in their lifetimes which is tax-free. "But that is a bit awkward", the Tories say, "because we are running kind of short of cash. We are going to have to find a way to make up the shortfall. We'll do away with the indexing on old age pensions. That is how we'll do it", so the top 5 per cent can accumulate this $500,000 and pay no tax but the old age pensioner, by God, they will have to pay for it. That is the Government.
Then it has the nerve, Mr. Chairman, to ask us to let it borrow more money, And while it is borrowing more money it is decrying all of the borrowing which took place before. Here is this Government asking us to give it more and at the same time telling us that the evil in this society is that it has had to borrow so much. So the Government decides that what it will have to do is raise the taxes on ordinary Canadians. So what did it do? It upped the sales tax. But Government was careful when it upped the sales tax because it knew that a sales tax works harder on average income Canadians than it does on those at the upper-income levels. That is typically Tory. That is the kind of thing which one could have anticipated would occur but hoped would not. It is a tradition of the Conservative Party; sock it to those who don't have much. Give it to those who have more than they need. That has been the tradition of the Conservative Party in Canada and of Conservative Parties all around the world. To think, Mr. Chairman, that they would have the nerve to come back and ask to borrow more.

The Minister of National Health and Welfare has the answer to everything. He walks around almost blind. He stands in his place and defends the indefensible. He is the only person in the caucus of the Tory Party who is still arguing that it is good to deindex pensions. The Prime Minister has not given him the word yet.
If that isn't bad enough, last Friday, and a month ago, he was going around the country saying that because of the high deficit, and because we are in such debt, we must look at new ways of funding health care. He thinks perhaps we should be looking at privatizing the health care system so the Government does not have to pay out as much, and will have more to give to its rich friends. So what has now started is a movement.
We have the Minister of National Health and Welfare who speaks to the medical association, I believe in Alberta, and says he wants it to consider the possibility of moving towards more privatization of the health care scheme in Canada. Because, after all, the Government cannot afford to carry the burden of providing universal health care to the poor, and the rich can afford it so they don't have to worry. The unfortunate part of it all, I say to your, Mr. Chairman, is that the end result of all of this will be that Government will not bring down the deficit, because it does not have the will to bring down the deficit, because it is afraid to go to where the problem really lies, and that problem really lies in the level and amount of give-aways which this Government and its predecessor Governments have made available to the private corporations.
My grandfather was a Conservative, God rest his soul.

Mr. Chairman, I have a number of questions for the Minister. Perhaps she could give us some explanations about the nature of the Borrowing Authority Bill we are discussing tonight.
In the statement the Minister of Finance gave when this Bill was introduced on May 28 he indicated that this $16.2 billion would bring the total borrowing authority for the current fiscal
June 17, 1985

year to $32.2 billion. He compared that to the total borrowing authority Parliament had granted to the two different Governments for 1984-85, which amounted to $31.9 billion. In effect, we are granting an additional $300 million this year. He indicated that while Parliament had granted borrowing authority of $31.9 billion last year, $27.6 billion was actually expended by the Government, leaving $4.3 billion unused as of March 31, 1985.
The request for borrowing authority this year is $300 million higher. Does that mean that $4.6 billion will be left in a fund for unspecified expenditures? Could the Minister tell us what the unspecified expenditures portion of this borrowing authority is likely to be by the end of this fiscal year?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I am not sure that I could estimate at this stage what the unused portion may be by the end of the year. I would indicate that the figures do not appear to be quite correct. I think that perhaps the $2.2 billion of short-term Section 39 borrowing has been included twice in that total, because the figures the Hon. Member was giving were not correct. I would have to check Hansard. Perhaps there was a mistake. I would like to put that on the record.
We will, of course, be trying to control our expenditures as much as possible and not use any further borrowing authority than is necessary. The total amount of borrowing authority will depend on the economic prospects we have, which at the moment we are reasonably pleased about, given the circumstances of the country. It will depend on interest rates which have been trending downward. It will depend on revenue projections. As more people continue to go to work we will have increased revenues. All of this will be reasonably positive in terms of the actual borrowing.

Borrowing Authority Act

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, what is the Government's interpretation of the amount of money that it can borrow under Section 39 of the Financial Administration Act? subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Could the Minister indicate the difference in cost for the 180 day borrowings versus the kind of borrowings that are normally carried out under the borrowing authority as such? speechtext: The interest rate spread changes every day. Between short and long it is normally about 1 per cent. However, you cannot always put everything in the least costly part of the market because that would jack up rates in that part of the market and would change the spread going in the other direction. That is why our debt management program of not using Section 39 is very important to us. We do try to design our debt management in order that the costs are minimized, depending on the rate spread at any given time in different sections of the market.

Borrowing Authority Act
height of the inflation cycle when nobody wanted to lend for long periods of time. Therefore, we have what is called a reverse yield curve, because everyone wants to keep their money very short.

Mr. Chairman, I will deal with the first point raised about the average interest rate. The reason that rate is historically quite high is that the deficit doubled over five or six years as interest rates were at their peak. Therefore, the accumulated debt is weighted to the high interest rates that had to be paid during that period when the former Government treated the deficit, its expenditures and revenue so irresponsibly. That constitutes a large part of that cost.
The amount of deferred corporate income taxes is to be found in Corporate Financial Statistics published by Statistics Canada. It is quite readily available during business hours. It is $29.4 billion for 1982, the latest year available.
Let me point out that the so-called interest on unpaid taxes is not relevant or applicable because deferred taxes arise out of the investment a company makes. It concerns capital cost allowances and therefore there is no deferral of taxes without an initial investment. Corporations, as citizens, pay the taxes that are owing. However, not only corporations but individuals can write off their interest costs if they invest money to some extent as well.

The concept that indexing everything is undesirable is a valid argument. 1 would accept, for example, if the Government said to those who are contracted by the Government that it would not automatically give them a 3 per cent or 4 per cent increase every year, in line with the rate of inflation.
1 would understand if the Government told them that they would have to fight for every penny. That is certainly argued in terms of labour-management negotiations. However, I found it objectionable to have the same argument apply, with such religious fervour, by Members of the Government, including the President of the Treasury Board and the Minister of Finance, when it comes to people who are no longer able to work an extra hour-and-a-half a week if their income begins to fall. The Government should find a way to provide a better service, which is more efficient and which would cut costs to keep them in line with government ceilings.
Senior citizens are not in the position to fight back. The bulk of them live in poverty or below the poverty line. It seems to me it is desirable for people who retire, who can no longer provide for their own needs by working, that indexing should continue to apply. I think that is a humane and sensible provision. Why is the Government out to punish Public Service employees who have worked 30 years for the Government of Canada? Why is the Government out to punish people who started their working careers for 20 cents or 40 cents a day back in the days of the Great Depression? They are now trembling. They do not know if the purchasing power of their pensions will get them through. Why is the Government picking on the people who are the weakest in society? If the Government wants to preach deindexation, why does it not do it to able-bodied individuals who are in their working years and to corporations and companies which have been ripping off the Government for a very long time?

I believe there is more consistency in our approach to the policies which we have produced than we have seen from any government for a long time. There is considerable sensitivity, concern and awareness.
We recognize that there is a short-term problem with the elderly poor, in which case those on the GIS are protected. We also recognize that there is a long-term problem in that these things will continue to happen if we do not provide for and encourage the kind of pension recommendations which are
Borrowing Authority Act
included in the Budget, such as pensions for part-time workers, earlier vesting and portability. All those things will help women, who comprise the larger proportion of our elderly poor.
We have very carefully balanced the policies we have outlined in the Budget. We have indicated that we would watch the trends very closely. It is something to which we are very sensitive. When we are in a position to do so, we will have more flexibility in social policy and we will be able to enrich some of the programs.
As I indicated earlier tonight, we have to ensure that the social policy meets the needs of the present and the future rather than the needs of the past. That means that we need flexibility, financial responsibility and fiscal responsibility. If we do not have that, we will come to the point where the funds will simply not be there to deal with the people who have real needs. I believe that people who have lived through the Depression and the wars know how important it is to take responsibility for the future. We are enormously sensitive to senior citizens and to other people who are in need in our society. That is why we indicated in the budget papers that we would watch the situation very closely with a view to enriching the programs as soon as we have the fiscal capacity to do so.

subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION-POSTAL DELAYS-REQUEST FOR POSTPONEMENT OF RATE INCREASES
CANADA POST CORPORATION-POSTAL DELAYS-REQUEST FOR POSTPONEMENT OF RATE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under Standing Order 45. On June 4 in the House, in the absence of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Beatty), I asked his Parliamentary Secretary if Cabinet should not be considering improving Canada Post services before a rate increase is approved and implemented. Clearly the Canadian economy cannot afford to ignore the deteriorating productivity in a Crown corporation, that is the Post Office, that vitally affects every Canadian and the ability of every Canadian business to compete effectivetly in the marketplace.
Canadians want quality service and there is no reason they should not receive it. They are paying for first-class service and are entitled to the best. Canada Post claims that the mail is on time in 86 per cent of cases. This is just not good enough
Adjournment Debate
in the estimation of most Canadians. Normally if a paying customer is dissatisfied with the services of a particular company he has the option of taking his business elsewhere where he can receive the best quality service for his money. Since the post office has a monopoly on first-class mail it is not possible to go elsewhere unless a person can afford the services of private couriers.
Why should Canadians be forced to do this? It is our responsibility to provide postal service to Canadians, and ultimately to provide the best service for their money. The cost of doing business through the post office is not just the cost of stamps, but also the cost of delays, uncertainty, and anxiety. It is not knowing what you are going to get in the mail and when you are going to get it. Canadians seem to be giving up hope of better postal service, Mr. Speaker. They are plain fed up and tired of giving Canada Post the benefit of the doubt. Canadians want a post office that reflects responsibility, dependability, and service consistency and efficiency.
How can a postal rate increase be justified when we are aware of the many horror stories about disgraceful service. 1 am not referring to isolated incidents. The public is now being asked to pay more for postage in an environment where volumes of addressed mail are declining along with the quality of service. The seeming inability of Canada Post to provide consistently good service will hobble its future. Canada Post stands to lose a tremendous volume of business to private courier services.
Surely the Corporation must realize that a price increase during a period of declining service can only accelerate the decline in mail volumes and ultimately result in additional revenue losses, something 1 am sure the Corporation does not want to have happen if it still intends to clear its deficit position by 1987. We must remember that the inefficiencies of Canada Post not only impact negatively on the general public of the country, but also cost the business community, particularly small business which can ill afford to have its time and money wasted and abused by Canada Post.
Not only are small businesses concerned about the two-cent rate increase for first-class mail, but also about the possibility of a larger increase for small packages that are not sent first class. If these rate increases are approved they could force lay-offs and closings among businesses that are unable to make the necessary changes in their operations before the increases come into effect. Indeed, it is no small wonder that small business owners get very upset at the slightest hint of a postal disruption.
It is truly unfortunate that Canada Post all too often appears to be threatening to strike or is suffering from labour trouble. Perhaps it is time to reconsider whether Canada Post should have the right to strike. I believe that it is an essential service. More importantly, should a corporation that is vital to millions of Canadians have the right to disrupt a service that could mean the livelihood of hundreds of thousands of Canadians?

June 17, 1985
Adjournment Debate
It is time to get Canada Post's house in order. It is time to consider what the customers want; that is, what Canadians expect and want for their money.
I commend Canada Post in its attempt to decrease and eventually eliminate its cash flow deficit. It is true that the Corporation has come a long way since its incorporation in 1981, but it is not fair to ask Canadians to carry the burden of its deficit when there is little indication and hope of improved services in the future. They are being asked to pay more for a service that is totally unacceptable.
In summary, I would ask my Cabinet colleagues to seriously consider the proposed Canada Post rate increases, what effect they will have on Canadians and whether they honestly feel Canadians should be asked to pay more for services while there is no evidence of improvement in the basic service. I have had many letters and phone calls to my constituency office about this topic. Not one letter has been complimentary of the post office. They have all been harshly critical of the service and demanding that we not approve a rate increase.
Finally, let me talk about the absenteeism rate at Canada Post. It is nowhere near the level in private enterprise. I believe it is another serious flaw that the management of the corporation should bring into line with normal levels. Perhaps when other efficiencies are put into effect, only then should it come back to the Government to ask for a rate increase.

subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION-POSTAL DELAYS-REQUEST FOR POSTPONEMENT OF RATE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to thank the Hon. Member for Don Valley East (Mr. Attewell) for providing Canada Post with copies of the envelopes that took a great deal of time to get to their destination. I can assure the Hon. Member that upon receipt of these envelopes, an investigation has been launched by Canada Post and the Corporation will determine the causes of the undue delay that occurred in the delivery process.
The Corporation and the Government recognize that perhaps one of the single most important issues for Members of Parliament and many Canadians is the level of service provided by Canada Post. In fact, I believe we could say that this is something that truly unites Canadians. In this, the Corporation achieved initial dramatic increases in the level of service, with speed and reliability levels reaching up to 90 per cent on-time performance in 1983-84.
However, several factors affected its performance in 1984 and earlier this year. One of the major factors is that the Corporation is now processing the largest volumes of mail in the history of the post office. Further, during the prolonged period of labour contract negotiations, many large and small postal users flooded the system to protect themselves from possible disruptions. This made Canada Post's task of providing Canadians with acceptable levels of service particularly difficult.
Since service is Canada Post's business, every effort is being made to restore service performance to previous levels. Recent tests indicate that this has been under way for the past two months and that service performance now stands at an 85 per
cent level. Canada Post Corporation's goal is to reach a 90 per cent on-time service performance level in the next few months. Of course, the Corporation will maintain its policy of both monitoring and publicly releasing its service performance levels on a regular basis.
In a corporation which handles more than 25 million pieces of mail every day; in a corporation which handles almost 7 billion pieces of mail every year, such incidents are bound to happen. If only 1 per cent of the mail does not get to destination on time, we have 250,000 unhappy customers.
Canada Post is conscious of the inconvenience this problem causes its customers and I can assure the Hon. Member for Don Valley East that all efforts are being made by the Corporation to reduce to a minimum these types of incidents, and at the least possible cost of Canadians.

subtopic: TRANSPORTATION OF DANGEROUS GOODS-RAIL CARRIAGE HAZARD TO TORONTO
TRANSPORTATION OF DANGEROUS GOODS-RAIL CARRIAGE HAZARD TO TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 24, the Railway Transport Committee of the Canadian Transport Commission rejected a recommendation to reroute trains carrying hazardous materials through the centre of downtown Toronto. That was a shock to me, a shock to my constituents, and a shock to the people of Metropolitan Toronto. That recommendation had been made by a very distinguished committee, the Burton-Post Committee. Burton is a professor at the University of Toronto and is well regarded; Post is actually the Ontario Regional Manager of the Railway Transport Committee itself. These two distinguished gentlemen recommended rerouting out of downtown Toronto trains carrying hazardous material. However, for some astounding reason, the Committee rejected this recommendation.
In addition, both myself and my constituents were shocked because the main line of both CPR and CNR go right through my constituency of York East. It is the same line on which the famous Mississauga train derailment occurred a few years ago. If that train had stayed on the track in Mississauga, that accident would have occurred 30 minutes later in my constituency. All the people in my constituency have been very concerned about this situation ever since that time. They are very concerned about train derailments because something like 1,500 freight cars carrying hazardous materials travel through Metropolitan Toronto every month. Two accidents occur involving those particular freight cars every year. The Mississauga train derailment was one example. Another accident occurred recently in February, 1984. It was an accident in which a so-called empty freight car blew up in the MacMillan Yard in the Scarborough area of Metropolitan Toronto. Since that time there have been a number of very famous train accidents, one occurring in the Barrie area of Ontario and another occurring in the Pembroke area of Ontario. Of course there was the very famous one in India. All those accidents involving trains carrying hazardous materials required a great evacuation of residents living in the surrounding areas.
June 17, 1985

The Commissioner of Roads and Traffic in Metropolitan Toronto indicated that it was impossible to have a similar evacuation in Metropolitan Toronto because of the high density population in that area. A number of suggestions have been made on how to deal with this sort of problem. One was to slow down freight trains to something like 25 miles per hour or 40 kilometres per hour. That has been rejected already by the Railway Transport Committee, because there are so many trains travelling this route it would clog up the line. The Committee indicated that it was impossible to slow them down and clog up the line.
Another suggestion, as I just indicated, was the rerouting of trains. That was rejected because of the cost of $120 million, apparently, to build other facilities to allow for the rerouting of these trains out of Metropolitan Toronto. By the way, these trains travel back and forth, carrying the same goods in and out, without dropping them off at all. It is an incredible situation.
The Toronto Board of Education has arranged for and is now holding evacuation drills in its schools. There are nine such schools in areas adjacent to the direct lines travelling through the Metropolitan Toronto area. There are something like 76,000 students in those schools. They had their first drill on March 5. They are planning another evacuation drill in the fall and expect to carry them out on a regular basis.
Other suggestions have been made about how to deal with the situation. Some of them include ceilings on the numbers of cars on these trains. Right now these trains carry up to 150 separate carloads of hazardous materials at a time.
Another suggestion for the federal Government or the Commission is to prepare some evacuation plans themselves. They have not done anything of that sort.
Another suggestion is to make sure that the cabooseless trains which are proposed to travel back and forth not be allowed to travel in high density metropolitan areas. There has been nothing said about that as yet.
Of course another suggestion is the colour-coding of these cars carrying hazardous material. That at least is apparently going to be introduced when the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act, proclaimed November 1, 1980, is actually put into effect. There are no regulations promulgated to put it into effect, but I understand those regulations will come in on July 1 of this year. They will finally be some colour-coding so fire-fighters will know what is in those cars when they turn over and cause these potentially hazardous situations.
The final suggestion was for not just a rerouting but a relocation of the actual tracks themselves; put them in an area where there would not be a high density of people and there would not be the same sort of problem situation occurring. Obviously there has been a lot of resistance to that because it will cost a lot of money, and there will be some people wherever the track is relocated. But it is possible because there is a green belt plan around metropolitan Toronto. It would be possible to relocate the track in that area. Approval has to
Adjournment Debate
come from the Cabinet, not from the Canadian Transport Commission or the Railway Transport Committee.
I ask the Parliamentary Secretary this evening if the Government is now prepared, if it is going to reject all of these other suggestions, to finally approve some funding for a relocation of these tracks to solve the problem and make sure the safety of 2.5 million people in metropolitan Toronto is protected, that they are not going to be placed in a situation such as the one which recently occurred in India where they suffered such devastation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul Dick (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: TRANSPORTATION OF DANGEROUS GOODS-RAIL CARRIAGE HAZARD TO TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 hope to respond to most of the items the Hon. Member has raised.
The question of transportation of dangerous commodities through populated areas, be they large or small, is one of grave concern to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski). As you know, it was the present Minister who asked Mr. Justice Samuel Grange to inquire into and report on the derailment at Mississauga in November of 1979. The Minister has followed this issue closely over the intervening years.
As a result of the Grange Commission inquiry, many important steps have been taken to increase the level of safety in the transportation of dangerous commodities through built-up areas. For instance, hot box detectors have been installed, gateway inspections are being performed, a retro-fit program is underway to install roller bearings, tank cars have been equipped with double-shelf couplers, regulations have been promulgated with respect to thermal and bottom fitting protection and new freight safety inspection regulations became effective on November 5, 1984. Hon. Members know that there has been much recent debate in this Chamber with regard to the transportation of dangerous goods and more specifically PCBs. New regulations enforcing standards for the transportation of dangerous goods will come into force July 1, 1985.
As to the case at hand, Mr. Speaker, as already stated by the Minister, the implications of the Burton-Post report recommendations are severe and there has not been a clear consensus as to which of the two, if any, should be implemented. I would like to advise the Hon. Member that the responsible authorities are invited to apply for railway relocation at any time, an option which has yet to be exercised. It must be pointed out at this time, Mr. Speaker, that the CTC has not rejected the recommendations of the Burton-Post report, but rather that in an effort to reach a solution which would prove satisfactory to all interested parties the CTC has invited submissions on safety measures not already addressed in the Burton-Post report. These submissions must be filed by October 1, 1985. I would encourage the interested parties to take advantage of this opportunity and make their views and ideas known.

June 17, 1985

subtopic: NATIONAL PARKS-PARKS POLICY-MINISTER'S POSITION. (B) REQUEST FOR MINISTERIAL ASSURANCE
NATIONAL PARKS-PARKS POLICY-MINISTER'S POSITION. (B) REQUEST FOR MINISTERIAL ASSURANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you probably know, on page 5642 of Hansard of June 11, in a question put to the Minister of Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) on Parks Canada, it is shown that 1 did receive a reply to the effect that the Minister committed herself to protecting, improving and beautifying the Parks. Having received that reply, I pressed her further to obtain a commitment that she would not review or change the present policy of Parks Canada, that there will not be any mining, timber cutting or other activities in conflict with Parks Canada policies.
In reply, apart from the fact that she could not resist the temptation of addressing some vilifying comments in my direction, comments which are on the record for anyone to see, she urged me to stop reading newspaper headlines and referred me to statements made before the standing committee of the House. She did this rather than taking a clear stand on whether or not she would make sure that there would be no review or change of the existing Parks Canada policies in which Canadians place so much confidence and have for many decades.
Today, what I see in The Globe and Mail is an article describing an interview with the Minister. This article again puts in jeopardy the attitude of the Government toward the environment, and in this case toward Parks Canada. In the article, it says that the Minister first indicated that she would not consider mining or logging in national parks like Banff or Jasper. Big deal. Of course one does not consider mining or logging in such parks as Banff or Jasper. What kind of a statement is that? It is a well known fact that those two major parks, along with others, represent a very valuable heritage. They are parks in which one would not even dream of let alone contemplate the possibility of mining or logging.
The interview goes on to quote the Minister as saying that it is not anything anyone would wish, but if they are to establish a park in an area where the logging and mining rights are owned by private developers, then there would have to be some compromise. What kind of a park would this be that the Government envisages? Is it a logging park, is it a mining park or is it a logging and mining park? How can one reconcile this kind of statement with the well established practices and policies of Parks Canada, which are to ensure that there are no activities of this kind?
For example, would this kind of proposal lead to the acquisition of South Moresby in those magnificent islands as a national park in which logging would be allowed? I would ask, as would you, Mr. Speaker, what kind of park that would be. Would it be a park in which the land is saved but not the forests? Does that make any sense?
I am amazed at this kind of muddled thinking that is emerging from the Government which does not seem to know the basics about environmental and parks policies. At this rate,
the Government is becoming a menace to the environment. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) cannot go on saying that the Minister was misquoted. That is like saying that a tape recorder was functioning improperly. We cannot go on like that. The series of statements indicates that something is profoundly wrong and that there is an attitude which poses a threat to the parks. It poses a threat to parks in the same way in which the Government posed a threat to wildlife by the cuts it made last November. On the one hand we have a Government which prides itself on the creation of jobs, but on the other hand it does not hesitate to wipe out existing jobs in wildlife. It still has the nerve to defend that decision, in light of the continuous appeals to restore the Canadian Wildlife Service.
The Government has already made decisions which pose a threat to another very important field which has environmental implications-renewable energy. Renewable energy is very important. It is the path to a conservation approach and to the use of resources which are not finite and environmentally friendly. It has taken years to put renewable energy resources on track. However, the NRC is having to abandon its research, as well as a group of scientists who were involved in soft energy studies. The Budget has imposed a federal sales tax on insulation material, and solar and wind equipment. If all the elements are put together, we see a general trend which is telling Canadians that their future lies only with oil and gas. That is not the road which Canadians should travel. The Government is dismantling many years of careful work, which was launched in the 1970s, particularly in 1977 when the country was hit with the second oil crisis.
We are seeing a threat to the parks policy because of the silly statements of the Minister. There is a threat which has emerged in the wildlife field. There is a threat and an impending serious consequence to the over-all conservation of energy by renewable sources, due to the decisions of the Government.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. M. Gurbin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: NATIONAL PARKS-PARKS POLICY-MINISTER'S POSITION. (B) REQUEST FOR MINISTERIAL ASSURANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome the opportunity to respond to the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) on behalf of the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Greni-er). I find the logic of the Hon. Member somewhat convoluted.
I think he will know that the parks policy, as it is now written, is a direct consequence of the 1979 Conservative Government when the present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) approved the policy during his term of office as Minister of the Environment.
When the Hon. Member speaks about parks policy he should be fair enough and logical enough to define the whole policy. He knows that the policy, as it is presently written, which he supported when he was Minister and which continues to be supported without reservation by this Government, does indeed include specific areas in which there is a preservation and conservation attitude.
However, we also have a commitment to support the kinds of activities which will respect the things which have been done
June 17, 1985

by local residents. Such is the case with timber harvesting in Gros Morne National Park in Newfoundland and trapping in Wood Buffalo National Park in Alberta and the Northwest Territories. Those activities were not stopped two years ago, they are still continuing. These are activities which seem reasonable to the local residents. It was agreed at that time when the parks were established that the activities would be permitted because of their importance to the local economy. Nor can we be insensitive to the economic and cultural importance of certain activities such as hunting and fishing to our native peoples. New parks in Canada's North will be established in such a way that the importance of these activities will be fully recognized.
Again, I would point to new parks, Mr. Speaker. We want new parks and we are going to have new parks, but we will have to have some sensitivity toward these things. I cannot believe that the Hon. Member opposite would not share that
Adjournment Debate
similar view if he were in fact still in Government and still Minister of the Environment.
This Government without question is firmly committed to maintaining the natural beauty and integrity of our national parks, parks which are famous worldwide, and deservedly so. Resource extraction will not be permitted within their boundaries. But we cannot turn a blind eye to the economic and cultural importance of certain activities to local residence and native people. I know, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of the Environment, who is now the Vice-Chairman of an OACD conference and will be going to Helsinki to sigh certain documents on behalf of Canada and the international community, supports that comment and that perspective totally.
